:::

The sixth exercise gives a large node more virtual nodes. Shares follow the counts.

::: {#exr-pt-capacity}
#### Heterogeneous nodes

Dynamo notes that "the number of virtual nodes that a node is responsible can decided based on its capacity" [@decandia2007dynamo, Sec. 4.2, p. 209]. With positions uniform and node $i$
holding $v_i$ of the $m = \sum v_i$ positions, prove that its expected share is $v_i/m$, and check for capacities $1, 1, 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The $m$ arcs ending at the $m$ positions are exchangeable and sum to $1$, so each has mean $1/m$; node $i$'s share is the sum of $v_i$ of them, with mean $v_i/m$ by linearity of
[expectation](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#def-expectation).

## Python

Mean shares over random rings with $v = (32, 32, 64)$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(22)
v = [32, 32, 64]; owners = np.repeat(np.arange(3), v); shares = np.zeros(3)
for _ in range(2000):
    p = rng.random(sum(v)); order = np.argsort(p); ps = p[order]
    arcs = np.diff(np.concatenate([[ps[-1] - 1], ps]))                # arc ending at each position
    shares += np.bincount(owners[order], weights=arcs, minlength=3)
print("mean shares", np.round(shares / 2000, 3), "| expected", [x / sum(v) for x in v])
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean shares [0.25  0.249 0.501] | expected [0.25, 0.25, 0.5]
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise measures how far a failed node's load spreads. With $v$ virtual nodes it reaches many successors.

::: {#exr-pt-failure-spread}
#### Where a failed node's keys go

On a ring of $n = 20$ nodes with $v$ virtual nodes each, count the distinct nodes that take over a failed node's arcs, for $v = 1, 4, 16, 64$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Each of the failed node's arcs passes to the owner of the next position clockwise, a node chosen almost uniformly among the other $19$; with $v$ arcs the number of distinct heirs is about
$19(1 - (18/19)^v)$: $1$, $3.6$, $11$ and $18.7$. With $v = 1$ one neighbour takes everything, Sinha's cascade.

## Python

The counts on random rings.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(23)
n = 20
for v in (1, 4, 16, 64):
    res = []
    for _ in range(200):
        own = np.repeat(np.arange(n), v)[np.argsort(rng.random(n * v))]
        nxt = np.roll(own, -1)
        heirs = set(nxt[own == 0]) - {0}
        res.append(len(heirs))
    print(f"v = {v:2d}: mean distinct heirs {np.mean(res):.1f} (estimate {19 * (1 - (18 / 19)**v):.1f})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
v =  1: mean distinct heirs 1.0 (estimate 1.0)
v =  4: mean distinct heirs 3.6 (estimate 3.7)
v = 16: mean distinct heirs 10.9 (estimate 11.0)
v = 64: mean distinct heirs 18.4 (estimate 18.4)
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise reconciles Xu and Liu on hot keys. One talks about keys, the other about one key.

::: {#exr-pt-hot-claims}
#### Does consistent hashing help with hot keys?

Xu lists among the benefits of consistent hashing that it can "mitigate hotspot key problem" for the celebrities [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 5, "Wrap up"]; Liu says that consistent
hashing does not solve "a key ... super hot targeting a shard" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5]. Which is right?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Both, about different things. Even partitioning makes it unlikely that *several* celebrities land on one node, so it mitigates hotspots made of many hot keys. A *single* key is always on one
node (and its replicas), whatever the scheme, so its load is not spread; only splitting the key (@exr-pt-hot-split) or caching does that.

## Python

Three hot keys on $16$ nodes: the chance that two share a node, and the load of the one hottest key, which is always on one node.

```{.python .run}
n = 16
print(f"P(some two of three hot keys share a node) = {1 - (15 / 16) * (14 / 16):.3f}; a single hot key's load is on 1 node always")
```

```{.text .run-output}
P(some two of three hot keys share a node) = 0.180; a single hot key's load is on 1 node always
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise redoes Sinha's modulo example. Removing a node changes the modulus.

::: {#exr-pt-sinha-mod}
#### Sinha's key

Sinha writes that if node 2 of four is removed, "the new server to process a request will be node 1 because 10%3 equals 1" [@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 5, "Boosting scalability"]. With
hash $10$, where was the key before, and what fraction of keys keep their node when four nodes become three?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Before: $10 \bmod 4 = 2$, node 2, the removed one; after: node 1. A key keeps its node when $x \bmod 4 = x \bmod 3$, which happens for $x \bmod 12 \in \{0, 1, 2\}$: a quarter of the keys.
Removing one node moves three quarters, not the quarter it held.

## Python

The count over one period of $12$.

```{.python .run}
print(10 % 4, 10 % 3, "| keep:", [x for x in range(12) if x % 4 == x % 3])
```

```{.text .run-output}
2 1 | keep: [0, 1, 2]
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise compares Dynamo's strategies by the membership each node stores. Strategy 1 grows with the ring.

::: {#exr-pt-membership}
#### Membership state

Under strategy 1 each node stores the token positions of all nodes, $S \cdot T$ entries; under strategy 3, the owner of each of $Q$ partitions. Compare for $S = 30$, $T = 100$ and $Q = 120$, and
explain Dynamo's report that strategy 3 "reduces the size of membership information maintained at each node by three orders of magnitude" [@decandia2007dynamo, Sec. 6.2, p. 216].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$3000$ token positions against $120$ owners: a factor $25$ here. The factor grows with $T$, since strategy 1 needs many tokens per node to balance load while strategy 3's balance comes from
equal partitions, so for equal balance strategy 1 needs far more tokens; Dynamo's three orders of magnitude are measured at equal load-balancing efficiency.

## Python

The two sizes.

```{.python .run}
S, T, Q = 30, 100, 120
print(f"strategy 1: {S * T} entries, strategy 3: {Q} entries, ratio {S * T / Q:.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
strategy 1: 3000 entries, strategy 3: 120 entries, ratio 25
```
::::
:::
::::

### How consistent hashing moves and spreads keys

Two numbers decide whether a partitioning scheme scales: the fraction of keys that move when a node joins, and how far the busiest node's share exceeds the mean. The theorem computes both for
random positions; Karger et al. prove the balance of a family with $\Theta(\log C)$ points per bucket with high probability [@karger1997consistent, Thm. 4.1], and the parts below give the exact
first and second moments.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-consistent-hashing}
#### Consistent hashing

Let $n$ nodes each have $v$ positions on the ring, the $m = nv$ positions independent and uniform on $[0, 1)$, and let $K$ keys hash to independent uniform points.

(a) (**Modular hashing**) If $h(x)$ is uniform on $\{0, \dots, M - 1\}$ and $n(n + 1)$ divides $M$, then $h(x) \bmod n = h(x) \bmod (n + 1)$ with probability $1/(n + 1)$: going from $n$ to $n + 1$
partitions moves a fraction $n/(n + 1)$ of the keys.

(b) Each node's share has mean $1/n$, so a node owns $K/n$ keys on average. When a new node with $v$ independent uniform positions joins, only keys whose owner becomes the new node move, and their
expected number is $K/(n + 1)$.

(c) With $v = 1$, the probability that some node's share exceeds $c\ln n/n$ is at most $n^{1 - c(n-1)/n}$.

(d) A node's share $S$ has variance $\operatorname{Var}S = \dfrac{n - 1}{n^2(nv + 1)}$, so its standard deviation relative to its mean is $\sqrt{(n - 1)/(nv + 1)} < 1/\sqrt v$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* We first describe the arcs. Label the $m$ arcs by the position that ends them (the position owns the arc from its predecessor to itself). Fix one position; it is uniform, and the arc ending
at it exceeds $s$ exactly when none of the other $m - 1$ positions falls in the arc of length $s$ before it, so $\mathbb P(G > s) = (1 - s)^{m-1}$ for $0 \leq s \leq 1$. Hence
$\mathbb EG = \int_0^1(1 - s)^{m-1}\,ds = 1/m$ and $\mathbb EG^2 = \int_0^1 2s(1 - s)^{m-1}\,ds = 2/(m(m + 1))$. The positions are independent and identically distributed, so the $m$ arcs are exchangeable:
every arc has this law and every pair of distinct arcs has the same covariance.

(a) Write $x = qn(n + 1) + r$ with $0 \leq r < n(n + 1)$; the residues of $x$ modulo $n$ and $n + 1$ are those of $r$. Since $n$ and $n + 1$ are coprime, the map $r \mapsto (r \bmod n, r \bmod (n+1))$ is a
bijection from $\{0, \dots, n(n+1) - 1\}$ onto pairs of residues (the Chinese remainder theorem). The pairs with equal entries are $(u, u)$ with $0 \leq u < n$, and $r = u$ is the residue mapped to each. So
exactly $n$ of the $n(n + 1)$ residues of each period have equal residues, a fraction $1/(n + 1)$ when $h$ is uniform over whole periods.

(b) A node's share is the sum of the $v$ arcs ending at its positions, with mean $v/m = 1/n$. Given the positions, each key lies in the node's arcs with probability equal to the share, so the expected
number of keys is $K\,\mathbb ES = K/n$. When a node joins, a key's owner changes only if the first position after it is now one of the new node's, and then the key moves to the new node; keys never move
between old nodes. The moved keys are thus those the new node owns, and on a ring of $n + 1$ nodes its expected share is $1/(n + 1)$, giving $K/(n + 1)$.

(c) With $v = 1$ a node's share is one arc, and $\mathbb P(G > x) = (1 - x)^{n-1} \leq e^{-x(n-1)}$. By the union bound of the [rules of probability](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#prp-probability-rules)
over the $n$ arcs, the probability that some arc exceeds $x = c\ln n/n$ is at most $n e^{-c\ln n\,(n-1)/n} = n^{1 - c(n-1)/n}$.

(d) One arc has $\operatorname{Var}G = \frac{2}{m(m+1)} - \frac1{m^2} = \frac{m - 1}{m^2(m + 1)}$. The $m$ arcs sum to $1$, so $0 = \operatorname{Var}\sum G_i = m\operatorname{Var}G + m(m - 1)\gamma$, where
$\gamma$ is the common covariance, and $\gamma = -\frac{1}{m^2(m + 1)}$. A share is a sum of $v$ distinct arcs, so
$$
\operatorname{Var}S = v\operatorname{Var}G + v(v - 1)\gamma = \frac{v(m - 1) - v(v - 1)}{m^2(m + 1)} = \frac{v(m - v)}{m^2(m + 1)},
$$
and with $m = nv$ this is $\frac{(n - 1)}{n^2(nv + 1)}$. Dividing the standard deviation by the mean $1/n$ gives $\sqrt{(n - 1)/(nv + 1)}$, which is below $\sqrt{n/(nv)} = 1/\sqrt v$. $\square$

Part (c) is an upper bound on the largest share with one position per node; the largest share is in fact of order $\ln n/n$, about $\ln n$ times the mean, which is why single positions balance poorly.
Part (d) is the remedy: the imbalance falls like $1/\sqrt v$, and @fig-thc-vnodes compares it with simulated rings.

![Standard deviation of a node's share relative to the mean share, against the number of virtual nodes per node, for $20$ nodes: the formula of the theorem (line) and simulated rings
(points).](figures/vnode_balance.svg){#fig-thc-vnodes width=65%}

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Part (a) on Xu's numbers. Four to five partitions moves four fifths.

::: {#exm-thc-mod}
#### Modular hashing from four to five

Part (a) with $n = 4$: a fraction $1/5$ of keys stays, $4/5$ moves; the run checks it on $10^5$ hashed keys.

```{.python .run}
import hashlib
h = lambda k: int.from_bytes(hashlib.md5(k.encode()).digest()[:8], "big")
keys = [f"k{i}" for i in range(10**5)]
print(f"fraction moved from 4 to 5: {sum(h(k) % 4 != h(k) % 5 for k in keys) / len(keys):.4f} (theory {4 / 5})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
fraction moved from 4 to 5: 0.8030 (theory 0.8)
```
:::

Part (b) on the same keys. A fifth node takes about a fifth.

::: {#exm-thc-join}
#### Consistent hashing from four to five

With $v = 64$ the new node takes a share near $1/5$ (part (d) puts one ring's share within about $11\%$ of it), all from the old nodes and none moving between them.

```{.python .run}
import bisect, hashlib
H = lambda s: int.from_bytes(hashlib.sha256(s.encode()).digest()[:8], "big") / 2**64
def owners(nodes, keys, v=64):
    pts = sorted((H(f"{n}#{i}"), n) for n in nodes for i in range(v)); pos = [p for p, _ in pts]
    return [pts[bisect.bisect_left(pos, H(k)) % len(pts)][1] for k in keys]
keys = [f"k{i}" for i in range(10**5)]
a, b = owners("ABCD", keys), owners("ABCDE", keys)
moved = [(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b) if x != y]
print(f"moved {len(moved) / len(keys):.4f} (theory {1 / 5}); all to the new node: {all(y == 'E' for _, y in moved)}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
moved 0.1731 (theory 0.2); all to the new node: True
```
:::

Xu's remark about the "k/n keys" is part (b). It is an average.

::: {#exm-thc-xu-kn}
#### "Only $k/n$ keys"

Xu quotes that with consistent hashing "only k/n keys need to be remapped on average, where k is the number of keys, and n is the number of slots" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 5]. Part (b) gives
$K/(n + 1)$ for a join to $n + 1$ nodes, the same to first order, and only in expectation: with $v = 1$ the new node's arc, and so the number of moved keys, varies widely.
:::

Part (c) predicts a large maximum share with one position per node. Simulation shows it near $\ln n$ times the mean.

::: {#exm-thc-max}
#### The largest arc

For $n = 1000$ and $v = 1$, the largest share averages about $7.5$ times the mean $1/n$, against $\ln 1000 = 6.9$; part (c) with $c = 2$ bounds the probability of exceeding $13.8/n$ by about $10^{-3}$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(24)
n = 1000
mx = []
for _ in range(200):
    p = np.sort(rng.random(n)); mx.append(np.diff(np.concatenate([[p[-1] - 1], p])).max())
print(f"mean of largest share x n: {np.mean(mx) * n:.2f}; ln n = {np.log(n):.2f}; bound at c = 2: {n**(1 - 2 * (n - 1) / n):.1e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean of largest share x n: 7.56; ln n = 6.91; bound at c = 2: 1.0e-03
```
:::

Part (d) gives the effect of virtual nodes. One hundred give about ten percent.

::: {#exm-thc-sd}
#### Virtual nodes and balance

For $n = 20$, the relative standard deviation is $\sqrt{19/(20v + 1)}$: $0.97$ for $v = 1$, $0.31$ for $v = 10$, $0.097$ for $v = 100$ and $0.031$ for $v = 1000$.

```{.python .run}
for v in (1, 10, 100, 1000):
    print(f"v = {v:4d}: relative sd {(19 / (20 * v + 1))**0.5:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
v =    1: relative sd 0.951
v =   10: relative sd 0.307
v =  100: relative sd 0.097
v = 1000: relative sd 0.031
```
:::

Xu quotes a measurement of the spread. Part (d) predicts it.

::: {#exm-thc-xu-measurement}
#### Xu's five and ten percent

"With one or two hundred virtual nodes, the standard deviation is between 5% (200 virtual nodes) and 10% (100 virtual nodes) of the mean" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 5]. Part (d) gives
$1/\sqrt{100} = 10\%$ and $1/\sqrt{200} = 7.1\%$ for many nodes: the first figure matches, the second is lower than random positions give.
:::

Karger's construction uses logarithmically many points per bucket. Its balance is part (d) with $v$ of order $\log C$.

::: {#exm-thc-karger}
#### Karger's points per bucket

"Assuming that the number of buckets in the range is always less than C, we will need $\kappa\log(C)$ points for each bucket", and the family is balanced: each bucket "is with high probability responsible
for no more than $O(1/|\mathcal V|)$ fraction of the interval" [@karger1997consistent, Sec. 4.2 and Thm. 4.1]. Part (d) quantifies the same effect by its variance.
:::

Dynamo measured imbalance in production. It falls with load.

::: {#exm-thc-dynamo}
#### Imbalance in Dynamo

A node was counted out of balance if its load deviated from the average by more than $15\%$; "during low loads the imbalance ratio is as high as 20% and during high loads it is close to 10%", explained
by the fact that "under high loads, a large number of popular keys are accessed" [@decandia2007dynamo, Sec. 6.2, p. 215]. Part (d) concerns shares of the key space; request imbalance adds the skew of key
popularity.
:::

A node that leaves hands its arcs to its successors. Only its keys move.

::: {#exm-thc-leave}
#### A node leaves

When a node leaves, each of its arcs joins the arc of the next position clockwise, so exactly its keys move, $K/n$ on average by part (b), and with $v$ positions they spread over several nodes
(@exr-pt-failure-spread).
:::

The photo service can size $v$ from part (d). Five percent needs about four hundred.

::: {#exm-thc-photo}
#### Sizing the photo ring

For $64$ metadata nodes and a relative standard deviation of $5\%$, part (d) needs $\sqrt{63/(64v + 1)} \leq 0.05$, that is $v \geq 394$: about $25\,000$ positions on the ring, a table of under
$1\,\mathrm{MB}$ that every client can hold.

```{.python .run}
import math
v = math.ceil((63 / 0.05**2 - 1) / 64)
print(f"v = {v}, positions {64 * v}, relative sd {math.sqrt(63 / (64 * v + 1)):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
v = 394, positions 25216, relative sd 0.0500
```
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the arc law of the proof. The tail of one arc is a power.

::: {#exr-thc-arc-law}
#### The law of an arc

Simulate $m = 10$ uniform positions and check $\mathbb P(G > s) = (1 - s)^{m-1}$, $\mathbb EG = 1/m$ and $\mathbb EG^2 = 2/(m(m + 1))$ for the arc ending at the first position.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The arc ending at a fixed position exceeds $s$ when the other $m - 1$ positions avoid an interval of length $s$, each independently with probability $1 - s$. The integrals of the proof give the moments.

## Python

The simulation.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(25)
m, T = 10, 200_000
p = rng.random((T, m)); x = p[:, 0:1]
G = ((x - p[:, 1:]) % 1.0).min(axis=1)                  # distance back to the previous position
print(f"P(G > 0.2) {np.mean(G > 0.2):.4f} vs {0.8**9:.4f}; EG {G.mean():.4f} vs {1 / m}; EG^2 {np.mean(G**2):.5f} vs {2 / (m * (m + 1)):.5f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
P(G > 0.2) 0.1347 vs 0.1342; EG 0.1003 vs 0.1; EG^2 0.01826 vs 0.01818
```
::::
:::

The second exercise adds $k$ nodes at once. The moved fraction generalises part (b).

::: {#exr-thc-k-join}
#### Several nodes join

Prove that when $k$ nodes join a ring of $n$, with all positions uniform, the expected number of moved keys is $Kk/(n + k)$, and compare with modular hashing from $n$ to $n + k$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

As in part (b), a key moves only to a new node, so the moved keys are those the $k$ new nodes own on the ring of $n + k$ nodes, each with expected share $1/(n + k)$; by linearity, $Kk/(n + k)$. Modular
hashing keeps a key only when the two residues agree: a fraction $1/(n + 1)$ for $k = 1$ by part (a), but half the keys for $k = n$, since $h \bmod n = h \bmod 2n$ exactly when $h \bmod 2n < n$.
Doubling is the one change that modular hashing handles as well as consistent hashing; every other change moves far more.

## Python

Doubling from $8$ to $16$ nodes, and adding one node to $8$.

```{.python .run}
import hashlib
h = lambda k: int.from_bytes(hashlib.md5(k.encode()).digest()[:8], "big")
keys = [f"k{i}" for i in range(10**5)]
print(f"modular 8 -> 16 moves {sum(h(k) % 8 != h(k) % 16 for k in keys) / len(keys):.3f} (consistent {8 / 16:.3f}); "
      f"8 -> 9 moves {sum(h(k) % 8 != h(k) % 9 for k in keys) / len(keys):.3f} (consistent {1 / 9:.3f})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
modular 8 -> 16 moves 0.499 (consistent 0.500); 8 -> 9 moves 0.889 (consistent 0.111)
```
::::
:::

The third exercise checks part (a) when $M$ is not a multiple. Hash spaces are powers of two.

::: {#exr-thc-mod-powers}
#### A power-of-two hash space

For $M = 2^{32}$ and $n = 10$, compute the exact fraction of $h \in \{0, \dots, M - 1\}$ with $h \bmod 10 = h \bmod 11$, and compare with $1/11$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Count the full periods of $110$ in $[0, M)$, each contributing $10$, and the partial period at the end separately. The fraction differs from $1/11$ by less than $110/M$, which is negligible.

## Python

The exact count.

```{.python .run}
M, n = 2**32, 10
full, rest = divmod(M, n * (n + 1))
count = full * n + sum(1 for r in range(rest) if r % n == r % (n + 1))
print(f"exact {count / M:.10f}, 1/11 = {1 / 11:.10f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
exact 0.0909090927, 1/11 = 0.0909090909
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise proves monotonicity. Karger lists it as the first property.

::: {#exr-thc-monotone}
#### Monotonicity

Karger et al. call a ranged hash function monotone if, when buckets are added, "an item may move from an old bucket to a new bucket, but not from one old bucket to another" [@karger1997consistent,
Sec. 4.1]. Prove that item 4's assignment is monotone.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Adding positions can only shorten the walk from a key to the first position clockwise. If the first position after $x$ is still an old one, it is the same old position as before, since no old position
was removed; otherwise it is new. So a key's owner is unchanged or new.

## Python

The check over random additions.

```{.python .run}
import bisect, random
random.seed(26)
own = lambda P, x: P[bisect.bisect_left([p for p, _ in P], x) % len(P)][1]
ok = True
for _ in range(200):
    old = sorted((random.random(), "old%d" % i) for i in range(10)); new = sorted(old + [(random.random(), "new")])
    for x in (random.random() for _ in range(100)):
        a, b = own(old, x), own(new, x)
        ok &= a == b or b == "new"
print("monotone in all trials:", ok)
```

```{.text .run-output}
monotone in all trials: True
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise chooses $v$ for a target. It inverts part (d).

::: {#exr-thc-choose-v}
#### Choosing $v$

Solve part (d) for the smallest $v$ giving a relative standard deviation of at most $\sigma$ with $n$ nodes, and evaluate for $\sigma = 0.1, 0.05, 0.01$ and $n = 10, 100$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$(n - 1)/(nv + 1) \leq \sigma^2$ gives $v \geq ((n - 1)/\sigma^2 - 1)/n$, close to $1/\sigma^2$ for large $n$: about $100$, $400$ and $10^4$.

## Python

The table.

```{.python .run}
import math
for n in (10, 100):
    print(f"n = {n}: " + ", ".join(f"sigma {s}: v = {math.ceil(((n - 1) / s**2 - 1) / n)}" for s in (0.1, 0.05, 0.01)))
```

```{.text .run-output}
n = 10: sigma 0.1: v = 90, sigma 0.05: v = 360, sigma 0.01: v = 9000
n = 100: sigma 0.1: v = 99, sigma 0.05: v = 396, sigma 0.01: v = 9900
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise relates the share to the busiest node. A normal approximation is a guide.

::: {#exr-thc-max-load}
#### The busiest node

For $n = 100$ nodes, simulate the largest share relative to the mean for $v = 1, 10, 100$, and compare with $1 + 2.5\,\sigma_v$, where $\sigma_v$ is part (d)'s relative standard deviation (a rough
normal estimate of the maximum of $100$ shares).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With $v = 1$ the largest share is several times the mean (part (c)); with $v = 100$ it is about $1.25$ times, close to the normal guide, since a share is then a sum of many small arcs.

## Python

The simulation.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(27)
n = 100
for v in (1, 10, 100):
    mx = []
    for _ in range(100):
        p = rng.random(n * v); order = np.argsort(p); ps = p[order]
        arcs = np.diff(np.concatenate([[ps[-1] - 1], ps]))
        mx.append(np.bincount(np.arange(n * v)[order] % n, weights=arcs, minlength=n).max() * n)
    print(f"v = {v:3d}: largest share / mean {np.mean(mx):.2f}, guide {1 + 2.5 * np.sqrt((n - 1) / (n * v + 1)):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
v =   1: largest share / mean 5.11, guide 3.48
v =  10: largest share / mean 1.96, guide 1.79
v = 100: largest share / mean 1.27, guide 1.25
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise checks part (d)'s covariance. Arcs compete for a fixed total.

::: {#exr-thc-cov}
#### Negative covariance

Explain why two distinct arcs have negative covariance, and check $\gamma = -1/(m^2(m + 1))$ by simulation for $m = 5$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The arcs sum to $1$, so a long arc leaves less for the others. The proof derives $\gamma$ from $\operatorname{Var}\sum G_i = 0$: $-1/150 = -0.00667$ for $m = 5$.

## Python

The simulation.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(28)
p = rng.random((200_000, 5))
def arc(i):                                            # arc ending at position i: distance back to the previous position
    d = (p[:, i:i + 1] - p) % 1.0; d[:, i] = 1.0
    return d.min(axis=1)
print(f"cov of the arcs ending at positions 0 and 1: {np.cov(arc(0), arc(1))[0, 1]:.5f}, formula {-1 / (25 * 6):.5f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
cov of the arcs ending at positions 0 and 1: -0.00674, formula -0.00667
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise compares the bound of part (c) with simulation. The bound is loose by a constant.

::: {#exr-thc-bound-c}
#### How tight is part (c)?

For $n = 100$ and $c = 1.5, 2, 3$, compare $n^{1 - c(n-1)/n}$ with the simulated probability that the largest arc exceeds $c\ln n/n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The union bound counts every arc separately, and $(1 - x)^{n-1} \leq e^{-x(n-1)}$ adds a little; the simulated probabilities lie below the bound, within a small factor of it, so the bound captures the right
scale $c \ln n/n$.

## Python

The comparison.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(29)
n, T = 100, 50_000
p = np.sort(rng.random((T, n)), axis=1)
mx = np.max(np.diff(np.concatenate([p[:, -1:] - 1, p], axis=1), axis=1), axis=1)
for c in (1.5, 2, 3):
    print(f"c = {c}: simulated {np.mean(mx > c * np.log(n) / n):.5f}, bound {n**(1 - c * (n - 1) / n):.5f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
c = 1.5: simulated 0.08128, bound 0.10715
c = 2: simulated 0.00732, bound 0.01096
c = 3: simulated 0.00004, bound 0.00011
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise counts what a removal moves under modular hashing. It is Xu's rehashing problem in numbers.

::: {#exr-thc-xu-remove}
#### Removing one of four

Prove that going from $4$ to $3$ partitions under modular hashing moves a fraction $3/4$ of the keys, and compare with consistent hashing, where removing one of four nodes moves $1/4$ in expectation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Part (a) with $n = 3$ says the residues modulo $3$ and $4$ agree with probability $1/4$, so $3/4$ of the keys move. With consistent hashing only the removed node's keys move, $K/4$ on average by part (b)
(@exm-thc-leave).

## Python

The count over one period.

```{.python .run}
print("agree mod 3 and 4 for", sum(x % 3 == x % 4 for x in range(12)), "of 12 residues")
```

```{.text .run-output}
agree mod 3 and 4 for 3 of 12 residues
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise measures key counts rather than shares. Finite $K$ adds binomial noise.

::: {#exr-thc-key-noise}
#### Keys, not arcs

Given a node's share $S$, its number of keys is binomial with parameters $K$ and $S$. Prove that the relative variance of the key count is part (d)'s plus approximately $n/K$, and evaluate for $n = 64$,
$v = 400$ and $K = 3.65 \times 10^{10}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By the law of total variance, $\operatorname{Var}X = \mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(X \mid S) + \operatorname{Var}\mathbb E(X \mid S) = \mathbb E[KS(1 - S)] + K^2\operatorname{Var}S$. Dividing by $(K/n)^2$
gives $n^2\operatorname{Var}S$ plus about $n/K$ (from $\mathbb E[KS] = K/n$). For the photo service $n/K = 1.8 \times 10^{-9}$, negligible against $(0.05)^2$: the imbalance comes from the ring, not from the
keys.

## Python

The two terms.

```{.python .run}
n, v, K = 64, 400, 3.65e10
print(f"ring term {(n - 1) / (n * v + 1):.2e}, key term {n / K:.2e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
ring term 2.46e-03, key term 1.75e-09
```
::::
:::

## Secondary indexes and request routing {#sec-request-routing}

A partitioned store answers a lookup by its partition key at one node. Every other question, by another attribute or from a client that does not know where the key
lives, needs more machinery. Liu's driver table shows the first problem: "if you shard it by driver_id, each shard will likely have drivers with that location_id. When you
fetch drivers for a location_id, you need to scatter-gather all the shards" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Scatter/Gather"]. The second is the subject of what
Liu calls shard discovery: "a shard discovery tells you which shard a request belongs to and the shard node to forward the request to" (Ch. 5, "Shard Discovery"). This
section defines local and global secondary indexes and the three ways of routing a request.

For more on this topic, see @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5, "Sharding Considerations" and "Service Discovery and Request Routing"], @decandia2007dynamo [Secs. 4.5
and 4.8] and @chang2006bigtable [Secs. 5.1 and 5.2].

### Local and global indexes, and routing

An index on a partitioned table can follow the table's partitions or have partitions of its own. A router can sit in the client, in a separate tier, or in every node.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-request-routing}
#### Secondary indexes on partitioned data and request routing

1. A **local** (document-partitioned) secondary index is kept by each partition for its own rows. A query by the indexed attribute must ask every partition and combine the
   answers, a **scatter-gather**.
2. A **global** (term-partitioned) secondary index is itself partitioned by the indexed value. A query by one value asks one index partition; a write that changes indexed
   values must update the index partitions of the old and new values, often asynchronously.
3. A **partition map** records which node holds each partition. **Request routing** delivers a request to a node that holds its key, in one of three ways: any node accepts the
   request and forwards it; a **routing tier** looks the key up and forwards it; or a **partition-aware client** keeps a copy of the map and contacts the node directly.
4. A **location hierarchy** stores the partition map itself as a partitioned table, whose partitions are located by a smaller table, up to a root at a known place.
:::

::::

Dynamo describes the two client strategies of item 3: "route its request through a generic load balancer that will select a node based on load information, or ... use a
partition-aware client library that routes requests directly to the appropriate coordinator nodes", the second achieving "lower latency because it skips a potential forwarding
step" [@decandia2007dynamo, Sec. 4.5, p. 210].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Four SQLite files stand for four partitions of the photo table. A local index makes a query by tag ask all four.

::: {#exm-rr-local-index}
#### A local index

Photos are partitioned by `photo_id % 4`, and each partition indexes its own `(tag, photo_id)` rows; the photos tagged "harbour" are found by asking every partition.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3, random
random.seed(30)
parts = [sqlite3.connect(":memory:") for _ in range(4)]
for p in parts:
    p.execute("CREATE TABLE tags(tag TEXT, photo_id INT)"); p.execute("CREATE INDEX by_tag ON tags(tag)")
for pid in range(1000):
    parts[pid % 4].execute("INSERT INTO tags VALUES (?, ?)", (random.choice(["harbour", "market", "night", "sea"]), pid))
asked, hits = 0, []
for p in parts:
    asked += 1; hits += [r[0] for r in p.execute("SELECT photo_id FROM tags WHERE tag = 'harbour'")]
print(f"partitions asked: {asked}, photos found: {len(hits)}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
partitions asked: 4, photos found: 261
```
:::

A global index is partitioned by the tag. The same query asks one partition.

::: {#exm-rr-global-index}
#### A global index

The index rows `(tag, photo_id)` are partitioned by a hash of the tag, so all "harbour" rows are in one index partition, while the photos stay partitioned by identifier.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3, random, zlib
random.seed(30)
index = [sqlite3.connect(":memory:") for _ in range(4)]
for p in index:
    p.execute("CREATE TABLE tags(tag TEXT, photo_id INT)")
part = lambda tag: zlib.crc32(tag.encode()) % 4
for pid in range(1000):
    tag = random.choice(["harbour", "market", "night", "sea"])
    index[part(tag)].execute("INSERT INTO tags VALUES (?, ?)", (tag, pid))
hits = [r[0] for r in index[part("harbour")].execute("SELECT photo_id FROM tags WHERE tag = 'harbour'")]
print(f"index partitions asked: 1 (partition {part('harbour')}), photos found: {len(hits)}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
index partitions asked: 1 (partition 2), photos found: 261
```
:::

Liu's driver locations are the standard case for item 1. The table is partitioned by driver.

::: {#exm-rr-liu-drivers}
#### Drivers by location

With the driver table partitioned by `driver_id`, "when you fetch drivers for a location_id, you need to scatter-gather all the shards. Scatter-gather is not as performant as if you
were to fetch it from a single shard" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Scatter/Gather"].
:::

Liu's shard discovery table is a partition map. Each shard lists two nodes.

::: {#exm-rr-liu-map}
#### A partition map

For keys $1$ to $100$ on three shards: keys $1$-$33$ on shard 1 at `node_1, node_2`, $34$-$66$ on shard 2 at `node_2, node_3`, $67$-$100$ on shard 3 at `node_1, node_3`, "usually ...
stored in a data store like a ZooKeeper" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Shard Discovery"]. The lookup is a binary search over the range boundaries.

```{.python .run}
import bisect
bounds = [33, 66, 100]; nodes = [("node_1", "node_2"), ("node_2", "node_3"), ("node_1", "node_3")]
get_node = lambda key: (bisect.bisect_left(bounds, key) + 1, nodes[bisect.bisect_left(bounds, key)])
print({k: get_node(k) for k in (1, 33, 34, 99)})
```

```{.text .run-output}
{1: (1, ('node_1', 'node_2')), 33: (1, ('node_1', 'node_2')), 34: (2, ('node_2', 'node_3')), 99: (3, ('node_1', 'node_3'))}
```
:::

Dynamo lets any node take a request. A node that is not a replica forwards it.

::: {#exm-rr-dynamo-forward}
#### Forwarding in Dynamo

"If the requests are received through a load balancer, requests to access a key may be routed to any random node in the ring. In this scenario, the node that receives the request will
not coordinate it if the node is not in the top N of the requested key's preference list. Instead, that node will forward the request" [@decandia2007dynamo, Sec. 4.5, p. 210].
:::

Dynamo avoids routing through several hops. Every node knows the whole ring.

::: {#exm-rr-zero-hop}
#### A zero-hop table

"Dynamo can be characterized as a zero-hop DHT, where each node maintains enough routing information locally to route a request to the appropriate node directly", because
"multi-hop routing increases variability in response times" [@decandia2007dynamo, Sec. 4, p. 209]; the routing information spreads by gossip, so "each storage node is aware of the token
ranges handled by its peers" (Sec. 4.8.1).
:::

Bigtable's partition map is a three-level hierarchy. It is item 4.

::: {#exm-rr-bigtable-hierarchy}
#### Bigtable's location hierarchy

"The first level is a file stored in Chubby that contains the location of the root tablet. The root tablet contains the location of all tablets in a special METADATA table. Each
METADATA tablet contains the location of a set of user tablets"; the root tablet "is never split—to ensure that the tablet location hierarchy has no more than three levels"
[@chang2006bigtable, Sec. 5.1, p. 4].
:::

Bigtable clients cache locations. A cold cache costs three round trips.

::: {#exm-rr-bigtable-cache}
#### Caching locations

"If the client's cache is empty, the location algorithm requires three network round-trips, including one read from Chubby. If the client's cache is stale, the location algorithm could take
up to six round-trips, because stale cache entries are only discovered upon misses" [@chang2006bigtable, Sec. 5.1, p. 4]. Clients are partition-aware, and "most clients never communicate
with the master" (Sec. 5).
:::

Liu weighs a central router against partition-aware clients. Latency against freshness.

::: {#exm-rr-liu-options}
#### Central service or aware client

A central service gives "simplicity", but "additional latency to make an interprocess call" and is "difficult to scale"; a node-aware client improves latency but brings "the complexity of updating
the client mapping every time the configuration is changed", and "the consistency may suffer if the push to the client upon config update is delayed" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5,
"Option 1" and "Option 2"].
:::

A scatter-gather waits for the slowest partition. Chapter 1 computed the cost.

::: {#exm-rr-fan-out}
#### The tail of a scatter-gather

A query that asks all $n$ partitions completes when the last one answers, so by @prp-fan-out-tail its probability of exceeding $t$ is $1 - (1 - p)^n$ when each partition exceeds $t$ with
probability $p$: with $p = 0.01$ and $n = 64$ partitions, $47\%$ of the queries are slow.

```{.python .run}
print(f"P(slow) = {1 - 0.99**64:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
P(slow) = 0.474
```
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks Bigtable's capacity claim. One kilobyte per row and $128$ megabytes per tablet are the inputs.

::: {#exr-rr-bigtable-capacity}
#### $2^{34}$ tablets

"Each METADATA row stores approximately 1KB of data in memory. With a modest limit of 128 MB METADATA tablets, our three-level location scheme is sufficient to address $2^{34}$ tablets (or
$2^{61}$ bytes in 128 MB tablets)" [@chang2006bigtable, Sec. 5.1, p. 4]. Derive both numbers.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A METADATA tablet of $2^{27}$ bytes holds $2^{27}/2^{10} = 2^{17}$ rows, each locating one tablet. The root tablet locates $2^{17}$ METADATA tablets, each locating $2^{17}$ user tablets:
$2^{34}$. At $2^{27}$ bytes per user tablet, $2^{61}$ bytes.

## Python

The arithmetic.

```{.python .run}
rows = 2**27 // 2**10
print(f"rows per METADATA tablet 2^{rows.bit_length() - 1}; tablets 2^{(rows * rows).bit_length() - 1}; bytes 2^{(rows * rows * 2**27).bit_length() - 1}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
rows per METADATA tablet 2^17; tablets 2^34; bytes 2^61
```
::::
:::

The second exercise prices the writes of a global index. Each changed value touches a partition.

::: {#exr-rr-global-writes}
#### Writes to a global index

A photo with $5$ tags is uploaded, and later its tags are replaced by $5$ new ones. With the global index of @exm-rr-global-index over $64$ partitions, bound the index partitions each operation
touches, and compare with a local index.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The upload writes $5$ index rows, in up to $5$ partitions; the replacement deletes $5$ and inserts $5$, up to $10$. A local index writes only the photo's own partition, one partition for both
operations, but every query by tag then asks all $64$. Global indexes move cost from reads to writes.

## Python

The expected number of distinct partitions for $5$ and $10$ random tags.

```{.python .run}
n = 64
for k in (5, 10):
    print(f"{k} tags: {n * (1 - (1 - 1 / n)**k):.2f} distinct partitions on average")
```

```{.text .run-output}
5 tags: 4.85 distinct partitions on average
10 tags: 9.33 distinct partitions on average
```
::::
:::

The third exercise computes the latency of the three routing options. Hops cost round trips.

::: {#exr-rr-hops}
#### Hops

With $0.5\,\mathrm{ms}$ per network hop inside a data centre, compare the latency added by routing through a random node (which is a replica of the key with probability $N/S$, $N = 3$, $S = 30$
nodes), through a routing tier, and from a partition-aware client.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A random node forwards unless it is a replica: one extra hop with probability $1 - 3/30 = 0.9$, so $0.45\,\mathrm{ms}$ on average. A routing tier always adds one hop, $0.5\,\mathrm{ms}$.
A partition-aware client adds none, which is Dynamo's "skips a potential forwarding step".

## Python

The three averages.

```{.python .run}
hop, N, S = 0.5, 3, 30
print(f"random node {hop * (1 - N / S):.2f} ms, routing tier {hop:.2f} ms, aware client 0.00 ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
random node 0.45 ms, routing tier 0.50 ms, aware client 0.00 ms
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise handles a stale client map. The wrong node redirects.

::: {#exr-rr-stale-map}
#### A stale map

A partition moves from node 1 to node 2, and a client with the old map sends a request to node 1. Describe a protocol in which node 1 answers with a redirect carrying the new owner, and count the
round trips until the client's map is right again.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Node 1 knows it no longer owns the partition and replies "moved to node 2" instead of data; the client updates its map entry and retries at node 2. The first request costs two round trips; later
ones one. This is how Bigtable's stale cache entries "are only discovered upon misses".

## Python

The client loop.

```{.python .run}
owner = {"p7": "node2"}                                      # the truth
client_map = {"p7": "node1"}                                 # stale
def request(part):
    trips = 0
    while True:
        node = client_map[part]; trips += 1
        if owner[part] == node:
            return trips
        client_map[part] = owner[part]                       # redirect carries the new owner
print("first request:", request("p7"), "round trips; second:", request("p7"))
```

```{.text .run-output}
first request: 2 round trips; second: 1
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise designs the photo service's partitioning and its indexes. The feed is the hard query.

::: {#exr-rr-photo}
#### Partitioning the photo service

Partition `photos` by `owner_id`. Which queries are single-partition: the profile page, one photo by `photo_id`, the photos with a tag, the feed of a user who follows $200$ others?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The profile page is single-partition. A photo by identifier needs the owner: either embed the owner's partition in the identifier or keep a global index from
`photo_id` to owner. Tags need a global index or a scatter-gather. The feed reads up to $200$ owners' partitions, a scatter-gather over the followees, which is why feeds are usually
precomputed.

## Python

The partitions touched by a feed over $64$ partitions.

```{.python .run}
n, k = 64, 200
print(f"expected distinct partitions for {k} followees: {n * (1 - (1 - 1 / n)**k):.1f} of {n}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
expected distinct partitions for 200 followees: 61.3 of 64
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise asks what an asynchronous global index shows after a write. Read-after-write can fail.

::: {#exr-rr-index-lag}
#### A lagging index

A user tags a photo "harbour" and immediately searches for "harbour". The global index is updated asynchronously with exponential lag of mean $200\,\mathrm{ms}$, and the search comes $100\,\mathrm{ms}$
after the write. What is the probability that the photo is missing, and what does that mean for read-after-write consistency (@def-leader-follower)?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$\mathbb P(\text{lag} > 0.1) = e^{-0.5} = 0.61$: most such searches miss the new tag. The index is a replica of derived data, and its lag breaks read-after-write consistency for queries that go
through it, even when the photo table itself is consistent.

## Python

The probability.

```{.python .run}
import math
print(f"P(missing) = {math.exp(-0.1 / 0.2):.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
P(missing) = 0.607
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise sizes the routing table of a zero-hop ring. Every node holds it.

::: {#exr-rr-table-size}
#### A zero-hop table

A ring of $1000$ nodes with $256$ virtual nodes each stores, for every position, $8$ bytes of position and $4$ bytes of node identifier. Find the table size per node and the time to send it to a new
node at $100\,\mathrm{MB/s}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$256\,000$ positions of $12$ bytes, $3.1\,\mathrm{MB}$, sent in $31\,\mathrm{ms}$: small enough for every node and every client to hold, which is what makes zero-hop routing practical.

## Python

The size.

```{.python .run}
b = 1000 * 256 * 12
print(f"{b / 1e6:.2f} MB, {1e3 * b / 100e6:.0f} ms to send")
```

```{.text .run-output}
3.07 MB, 31 ms to send
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise bounds a scatter-gather's tail with replicas. Ask two replicas of each partition and take the first answer.

::: {#exr-rr-hedge}
#### Hedging a scatter-gather

In @exm-rr-fan-out, ask two replicas of each partition and use the faster. If replicas are slow independently with probability $0.01$, find the probability that the whole query is slow.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A partition is slow only if both replicas are, probability $10^{-4}$; the query is slow with probability $1 - (1 - 10^{-4})^{64} = 0.0064$, down from $0.47$, at the cost of twice the requests.

## Python

Both probabilities.

```{.python .run}
print(f"single {1 - 0.99**64:.4f}, hedged {1 - (1 - 0.01**2)**64:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
single 0.4744, hedged 0.0064
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise computes Bigtable's worst-case location cost. Stale entries are found by misses.

::: {#exr-rr-bigtable-stale}
#### Six round trips

Explain why a client whose cached locations are all stale needs up to six round trips: three to discover that the cached entries at each level are wrong, and three to read the correct ones.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The client tries the cached user tablet location and misses (one), then the cached METADATA tablet location and misses (two), then the cached root location and misses (three); it then reads Chubby
for the root (four), the root for the METADATA tablet (five) and the METADATA tablet for the user tablet (six). An empty cache skips the three misses.

## Python

The count.

```{.python .run}
levels = 3
print("empty cache:", levels, "round trips; stale cache:", 2 * levels)
```

```{.text .run-output}
empty cache: 3 round trips; stale cache: 6
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise chooses between local and global indexes by workload. Reads against writes.

::: {#exr-rr-choose}
#### Local or global

A tag index over $64$ partitions receives $10^3$ tag queries and $2 \times 10^4$ tag writes per second. Count the partition operations per second under each index, assuming $5$ tags per write.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Local: queries $64 \times 10^3$ plus writes $2 \times 10^4$ (one partition each), $8.4 \times 10^4$. Global: queries $10^3$ plus writes $2 \times 10^4 \times 4.8$ (distinct partitions per write),
about $9.7 \times 10^4$. Here the write-heavy workload favours the local index, slightly; the photo service, which reads far more than it writes, would favour the global one.

## Python

The totals.

```{.python .run}
n, q, w, t = 64, 1e3, 2e4, 5
local = q * n + w
glob = q + w * n * (1 - (1 - 1 / n)**t)
print(f"local {local:.2e}, global {glob:.2e} partition operations per second")
```

```{.text .run-output}
local 8.40e+04, global 9.79e+04 partition operations per second
```
::::
:::
::::

## Failure detection and membership {#sec-failure-detection}

Every mechanism of the chapter acts on failures it must first notice: a failover needs to know that the leader is gone, a sloppy quorum needs to know which nodes are
healthy, a ring needs to know who its members are. A node cannot tell a crashed peer from a slow one, so failure detection is a matter of timeouts, and Xu's first rule is
caution: "it is insufficient to believe that a server is down because another server says so. Usually, it requires at least two independent sources of information to mark
a server down" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 6, "Failure detection"]. This section defines heartbeat failure detectors and gossip membership, and proves how quickly a
heartbeat detector notices a crash and how rarely it suspects a live node.

For more on this topic, see @SystemDesignInterview2021 [Ch. 6, "Handling failures"], @decandia2007dynamo [Sec. 4.8], @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Secs. 3.5.1 and 3.5.4,
pp. 67-70], @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 5, "Ring membership promotion for failure detection"] and @chang2006bigtable [Sec. 5.2].

### Heartbeats, suspicion and gossip

A failure detector is a module that outputs suspicions. Its quality is measured by two properties, and gossip is the cheapest way to share what it learns.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-failure-detector}
#### Failure detectors and gossip membership

1. A **failure detector** at a node $o$ outputs, at each time, a set of nodes it **suspects** of having crashed. It is **complete** if every crashed node is eventually suspected
   permanently by every correct node, and **accurate** if no correct node is suspected.
2. A **heartbeat detector** has each monitored node $p$ send a **heartbeat** every $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ seconds; $o$ suspects $p$ when it has received no heartbeat from $p$ for
   a **timeout** $\theta$, and stops suspecting it when a heartbeat arrives.
3. A **gossip protocol** proceeds in rounds: in each round every node sends its state to one or more peers chosen at random, and a node that receives a state merges it into
   its own.
4. In **gossip membership**, a node's state is a **membership list** of (member, heartbeat counter, time of last increase) entries; each node increments its own counter
   periodically, merges by keeping the larger counter of each member, and considers a member failed when its counter has not increased for a period $T_{\mathrm{fail}}$.
   **Seed** nodes, known to all, ensure that every node eventually merges with every other's state.
:::

::::

Item 4 is Xu's protocol: "each node maintains a node membership list, which contains member IDs and heartbeat counters", "each node periodically sends heartbeats to a set
of random nodes, which in turn propagate to another set of nodes", and "if the heartbeat has not increased for more than predefined periods, the member is considered as
offline" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 6, "Failure detection"]. The heartbeat interval $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ is the one of the web-stack chapter's long-lived connections
(@def-real-time-delivery).

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Xu's membership list shows item 4 in one picture. One member's counter has stopped.

::: {#exm-fd-xu-list}
#### A stalled counter

"Node s0 notices that node s2's (member ID = 2) heartbeat counter has not increased for a long time", and "sends heartbeats that include s2's info to a set of random nodes. Once
other nodes confirm that s2's heartbeat counter has not been updated for a long time, node s2 is marked down" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 6, "Failure detection"].
:::

All-to-all heartbeats are simple and quadratic. Tan and Xu both say so.

::: {#exm-fd-full-mesh}
#### Full mesh

In a full mesh "every host in the cluster has the address of every other host and broadcasts messages to all of them"; "the number of messages grows quadratically with the number
of hosts" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.5.1, p. 67]. Xu: all-to-all multicasting "is inefficient when many servers are in the system" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 6].
For $1000$ nodes and one heartbeat per second each, a full mesh sends about $10^6$ messages a second; gossip to one peer sends $1000$.
:::

Dynamo propagates membership by gossip once a second. Peers are random.

::: {#exm-fd-dynamo-gossip}
#### Membership in Dynamo

"A gossip-based protocol propagates membership changes and maintains an eventually consistent view of membership. Each node contacts a peer chosen at random every second and the two
nodes efficiently reconcile their persisted membership change histories" [@decandia2007dynamo, Sec. 4.8.1, p. 212].
:::

Dynamo's failure detection is local. A node suspects a peer that does not answer it.

::: {#exm-fd-dynamo-local}
#### A local notion of failure

"A purely local notion of failure detection is entirely sufficient: node A may consider node B failed if node B does not respond to node A's messages (even if B is responsive to
node C's messages)"; client traffic plays the part of heartbeats, and "A periodically retries B to check for the latter's recovery" [@decandia2007dynamo, Sec. 4.8.3, p. 213].
:::

Seeds prevent a ring from splitting into rings that do not know each other. Dynamo explains how.

::: {#exm-fd-seeds}
#### Seeds

If an administrator joins A and then B to the ring, "nodes A and B would each consider itself a member of the ring, yet neither would be immediately aware of the other. To prevent
logical partitions, some Dynamo nodes play the role of seeds"; "because all nodes eventually reconcile their membership with a seed, logical partitions are highly unlikely"
[@decandia2007dynamo, Sec. 4.8.2, p. 213].
:::

Bigtable detects tablet-server failure through a lock service. Losing the lock means stopping.

::: {#exm-fd-bigtable}
#### Locks as liveness

"When a tablet server starts, it creates, and acquires an exclusive lock on, a uniquely-named file in a specific Chubby directory"; "a tablet server stops serving its tablets if it
loses its exclusive lock". The master "periodically asks each tablet server for the status of its lock", and if it cannot reach a server it takes the lock itself and deletes the
file, so that the server "can never serve again" [@chang2006bigtable, Sec. 5.2, pp. 4-5].
:::

Gossip spreads a rumour in about logarithmically many rounds. The run counts rounds for push gossip.

::: {#exm-fd-gossip-rounds}
#### How fast gossip spreads

In push gossip each informed node tells one random other node per round. For $n = 1000$ nodes the run needs about $18$ rounds, close to $\log_2 n + \ln n = 16.9$; the informed set roughly
doubles at first and the last few nodes take a few extra rounds.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(31)
def rounds(n):
    informed = np.zeros(n, bool); informed[0] = True; r = 0
    while not informed.all():
        senders = np.flatnonzero(informed)
        targets = (senders + rng.integers(1, n, senders.size)) % n       # a random other node
        informed[targets] = True; r += 1
    return r
print(f"n = 1000: mean rounds {np.mean([rounds(1000) for _ in range(200)]):.1f}; log2 n + ln n = {np.log2(1000) + np.log(1000):.1f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
n = 1000: mean rounds 18.0; log2 n + ln n = 16.9
```
:::

Sinha describes membership histories reconciled by gossip. Every node eventually knows every change.

::: {#exm-fd-sinha}
#### Membership histories

"Planned commissioning and decommissioning of nodes lead to membership changes. These changes form a history, recorded persistently on each node's storage and reconciled among ring
members using a gossip protocol"; "eventually, every node becomes aware of every other node's information" [@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 5].
:::

Gossip merges by maximum. The membership list is a CRDT.

::: {#exm-fd-merge}
#### Merging lists

Merging two membership lists by the larger counter of each member is the componentwise maximum of @def-happens-before item 5, so merges in any order converge, and a counter, once
heard of, is never forgotten.

```{.python .run}
a = {"s0": 12, "s1": 7, "s2": 3}; b = {"s0": 10, "s1": 9, "s3": 1}
merge = lambda x, y: {k: max(x.get(k, 0), y.get(k, 0)) for k in x.keys() | y.keys()}
print(sorted(merge(a, b).items()), "| order irrelevant:", merge(a, b) == merge(b, a))
```

```{.text .run-output}
[('s0', 12), ('s1', 9), ('s2', 3), ('s3', 1)] | order irrelevant: True
```
:::

Dynamo keeps transient failures out of the ring. Only explicit commands change membership.

::: {#exm-fd-explicit}
#### Explicit joins and leaves

"A node outage rarely signifies a permanent departure and therefore should not result in rebalancing of the partition assignment or repair of the unreachable replicas", so "an
administrator uses a command line tool or a browser ... to join a node to a ring or remove a node from a ring" [@decandia2007dynamo, Sec. 4.8.1, p. 212]. Suspicion changes where
requests go; membership changes where data lives.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise counts heartbeat messages. Gossip is linear.

::: {#exr-fd-messages}
#### Messages per second

Compare the heartbeat messages per second of a full mesh and of gossip to $f = 3$ random peers, for $n = 100$, $1000$ and $10^4$ nodes, each sending once per second.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Full mesh: $n(n - 1)$ messages per second; gossip: $fn$. At $10^4$ nodes, $10^8$ against $3 \times 10^4$. Gossip messages are larger, since they carry the whole list, which is why Dynamo
reconciles "histories" efficiently rather than sending everything.

## Python

The table.

```{.python .run}
for n in (100, 1000, 10_000):
    print(f"n = {n:6d}: full mesh {n * (n - 1):.1e}, gossip {3 * n:.1e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
n =    100: full mesh 9.9e+03, gossip 3.0e+02
n =   1000: full mesh 1.0e+06, gossip 3.0e+03
n =  10000: full mesh 1.0e+08, gossip 3.0e+04
```
::::
:::

The second exercise studies the growth of gossip rounds with $n$. The logarithm shows in a table.

::: {#exr-fd-gossip-growth}
#### Rounds against size

Run the push gossip of @exm-fd-gossip-rounds for $n = 10, 100, 1000, 10^4$ and compare the mean number of rounds with $\log_2 n + \ln n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The rounds grow by a constant each time $n$ is multiplied by ten, as a logarithm does, and stay close to $\log_2 n + \ln n$: the doubling phase takes about $\log_2 n$ rounds and the final phase,
in which uninformed nodes are found by chance, about $\ln n$.

## Python

The table.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(32)
def rounds(n):
    informed = np.zeros(n, bool); informed[0] = True; r = 0
    while not informed.all():
        s = np.flatnonzero(informed); informed[(s + rng.integers(1, n, s.size)) % n] = True; r += 1
    return r
for n in (10, 100, 1000, 10_000):
    print(f"n = {n:6d}: rounds {np.mean([rounds(n) for _ in range(50)]):5.1f}, log2 n + ln n = {np.log2(n) + np.log(n):5.1f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
n =     10: rounds   6.1, log2 n + ln n =   5.6
n =    100: rounds  11.8, log2 n + ln n =  11.2
n =   1000: rounds  18.2, log2 n + ln n =  16.9
n =  10000: rounds  23.9, log2 n + ln n =  22.5
```
::::
:::

The third exercise proves the final phase of gossip shrinks geometrically. The expectation is exact.

::: {#exr-fd-endgame}
#### The final phase

In push gossip with $I$ informed and $U = n - I$ uninformed nodes, each informed node picks one of the $n - 1$ others uniformly. Prove that $\mathbb E[U_{\text{next}} \mid U, I] = U(1 -
1/(n - 1))^I \leq Ue^{-I/(n-1)}$, and deduce that once $I \geq n/2$, the expected number of uninformed nodes falls by a factor at least $e^{-1/2}$ per round.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

An uninformed node stays uninformed if none of the $I$ informed nodes picks it; each misses it with probability $1 - 1/(n - 1)$, independently, so it stays with probability $(1 - 1/(n -
1))^I$, and by linearity of expectation $\mathbb E U_{\text{next}} = U(1 - 1/(n-1))^I \leq Ue^{-I/(n-1)}$. With $I \geq n/2$, $I/(n - 1) \geq 1/2$. Since informed nodes stay informed, $I$ only
grows, so the factor applies to every later round, and after $r$ such rounds $\mathbb EU \leq ne^{-r/2}$, which is below $1/n$ when $r \geq 4\ln n$: then by Markov's inequality all nodes are informed
with probability at least $1 - 1/n$.

## Python

The exact one-round expectation against simulation for $n = 100$, $I = 60$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(33)
n, I = 100, 60
left = []
for _ in range(20_000):
    t = (np.arange(I) + rng.integers(1, n, I)) % n          # informed nodes are 0..I-1
    left.append(n - I - np.count_nonzero(np.unique(t) >= I))
print(f"simulated {np.mean(left):.3f}, formula {(n - I) * (1 - 1 / (n - 1))**I:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
simulated 21.747, formula 21.753
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise corrects Tan's description of DynamoDB. Vector clocks are not a gossip protocol.

::: {#exr-fd-tan-claim}
#### Gossip and vector clocks

Tan writes that "DynamoDB uses a gossip protocol called 'vector clocks' to maintain consistency across multiple data centers" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.5.4, p. 70]. Using
@def-failure-detector and @def-happens-before, say what each of the two mechanisms does in Dynamo.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Gossip (item 3) disseminates membership and token information between nodes [@decandia2007dynamo, Sec. 4.8]. Vector clocks (version vectors) label versions of one data item so that ancestors
and conflicts can be told apart (Sec. 4.4). They are different mechanisms for different data; the sentence conflates them, and the paper describes Dynamo, the 2007 system, not the later
DynamoDB service.

## Python

The two mechanisms side by side on toy data.

```{.python .run}
membership = [{"s0": 5, "s1": 2}, {"s0": 4, "s1": 3}]
gossip = {k: max(m.get(k, 0) for m in membership) for k in ("s0", "s1")}
versions = [{"Sx": 2, "Sy": 1}, {"Sx": 2, "Sz": 1}]
leq = lambda u, v: all(u.get(k, 0) <= v.get(k, 0) for k in u.keys() | v.keys())
print("gossip merges membership:", gossip, "| vector clocks classify versions:", "conflict" if not (leq(*versions) or leq(*versions[::-1])) else "ordered")
```

```{.text .run-output}
gossip merges membership: {'s0': 5, 's1': 3} | vector clocks classify versions: conflict
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise shows a logical partition without seeds. Two rings form.

::: {#exr-fd-no-seeds}
#### Two rings

Simulate gossip between nodes that only contact peers they already know. Start with two groups $\{A, B, C\}$ and $\{D, E\}$ that know only each other, run $50$ rounds, then add a seed $S$ known to
all and run again. Who knows whom?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Without a common acquaintance, no message ever crosses between the groups: two logical rings, Dynamo's logical partition. A seed known to everyone receives both groups' lists and passes them on,
and after a few rounds every node knows every other.

## Python

Gossip over the acquaintance graph.

```{.python .run}
import random
random.seed(34)
def run(knows, rounds=50):
    for _ in range(rounds):
        for n in list(knows):
            peer = random.choice(sorted(knows[n] - {n}))
            merged = knows[n] | knows[peer]
            knows[n] = set(merged); knows[peer] = set(merged)
    return {n: sorted(k) for n, k in knows.items()}
g1 = {n: set("ABC") for n in "ABC"} | {n: set("DE") for n in "DE"}
print("without seed:", run(g1))
g2 = {n: set("ABCS") for n in "ABC"} | {n: set("DES") for n in "DE"} | {"S": set("S")}
print("with seed:   ", run(g2))
```

```{.text .run-output}
without seed: {'A': ['A', 'B', 'C'], 'B': ['A', 'B', 'C'], 'C': ['A', 'B', 'C'], 'D': ['D', 'E'], 'E': ['D', 'E']}
with seed:    {'A': ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E', 'S'], 'B': ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E', 'S'], 'C': ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E', 'S'], 'D': ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E', 'S'], 'E': ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E', 'S'], 'S': ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E', 'S']}
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise chooses Xu's $T_{\mathrm{fail}}$. It must exceed the time a counter takes to spread.

::: {#exr-fd-tfail}
#### How long to wait

With $1000$ nodes gossiping once per second, a counter increase takes about $18$ rounds to reach everyone (@exm-fd-gossip-rounds). Why must $T_{\mathrm{fail}}$ exceed this spread time plus the
counter's increment period, and what does a smaller value cause?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A node far from $p$ in the gossip order hears of $p$'s latest increase up to the spread time late. If $T_{\mathrm{fail}}$ is shorter than that delay plus the increment period, a node can see $p$'s
counter stalled although $p$ is alive: a false suspicion that violates accuracy. A safe choice is a few multiples of the spread time, for example $60\,\mathrm{s}$ here.

## Python

The tail of the spread time from simulation, to set $T_{\mathrm{fail}}$ above it.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(35)
def rounds(n=1000):
    informed = np.zeros(n, bool); informed[0] = True; r = 0
    while not informed.all():
        s = np.flatnonzero(informed); informed[(s + rng.integers(1, n, s.size)) % n] = True; r += 1
    return r
r = np.array([rounds() for _ in range(300)])
print(f"spread rounds: mean {r.mean():.1f}, 99th percentile {np.percentile(r, 99):.0f}, max {r.max()}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
spread rounds: mean 18.0, 99th percentile 22, max 22
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise explains why a Bigtable server kills itself. It is the fencing of @exr-lf-epochs.

::: {#exr-fd-bigtable-fence}
#### Why stop serving

Bigtable's tablet server stops serving if it loses its lock, and "if the file no longer exists, then the tablet server will never be able to serve again, so it kills itself" [@chang2006bigtable,
Sec. 5.2, p. 4]. What would go wrong if a server that lost its Chubby session kept serving its tablets?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The master, unable to reach the server, deletes its file and reassigns its tablets. If the old server kept serving, two servers would serve the same tablet, split brain (@def-leader-follower item 4).
Tying the right to serve to holding the lock makes the master's suspicion safe even when it is wrong: a falsely suspected server stops on its own.

## Python

A server that checks its lease before each request.

```{.python .run}
lock_files = {"ts1"}
def serve(server):
    return "served" if server in lock_files else "refused: lock lost"
print(serve("ts1")); lock_files.discard("ts1"); print(serve("ts1"))
```

```{.text .run-output}
served
refused: lock lost
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise follows Xu's advice of two sources. Requiring two suspicions makes false suspicions rarer.

::: {#exr-fd-two-sources}
#### Two independent sources

If each of two observers falsely suspects a live node in a given minute with probability $10^{-3}$, independently, how often is the node marked down when both must agree, and what does the rule cost in
detection time?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Both suspect with probability $10^{-6}$ per minute instead of $10^{-3}$, by [independence](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#def-independence). A real crash is
marked only when the slower observer suspects it, so detection takes the maximum of the two detection times.

## Python

The rates per day.

```{.python .run}
print(f"one observer: {1e-3 * 1440:.2f} false marks per day; two must agree: {1e-6 * 1440:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
one observer: 1.44 false marks per day; two must agree: 0.0014
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise shows a network partition fooling every detector. Accuracy and completeness cannot both be had.

::: {#exr-fd-partition}
#### A partition

A network partition separates nodes $\{1, 2\}$ from $\{3, 4, 5\}$, and no node has crashed. What do heartbeat detectors on each side report, and which property of item 1 fails?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Each side stops receiving the other's heartbeats and, after $\theta$, suspects all of them: accuracy fails, since every suspected node is alive. A detector that never suspected would be accurate and
incomplete. With timeouts, a crash and a partition look the same from one side, which is why systems pair detection with fencing (@exr-fd-bigtable-fence) or majorities.

## Python

The suspicion sets after $\theta$.

```{.python .run}
sides = [{1, 2}, {3, 4, 5}]
for side in sides:
    other = set().union(*sides) - side
    print(f"nodes {sorted(side)} suspect {sorted(other)}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
nodes [1, 2] suspect [3, 4, 5]
nodes [3, 4, 5] suspect [1, 2]
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise adapts the timeout to observed delays. A quantile of the inter-arrival times is a common rule.

::: {#exr-fd-adaptive}
#### An adaptive timeout

Heartbeats are sent every second and arrive with a jitter whose last $1000$ samples are recorded. Set $\theta$ to the $99.9$-th percentile of the observed gaps plus a margin of $0.5\,\mathrm{s}$, and
compute it for normal jitter of standard deviation $50\,\mathrm{ms}$ and for a heavy-tailed jitter.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With normal jitter the gaps stay within a few hundred milliseconds of $1\,\mathrm{s}$, and $\theta$ comes out near $1.7\,\mathrm{s}$. A heavy tail stretches the high percentile and the timeout with it: the
detector becomes slower where the network is less predictable, trading detection time for accuracy automatically.

## Python

The two timeouts, using the empirical quantile of @prp-quantile-estimate.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(36)
normal = 1 + rng.normal(0, 0.05, 1000) - rng.normal(0, 0.05, 1000)
heavy = 1 + 0.05 * rng.standard_t(2, 1000) - 0.05 * rng.standard_t(2, 1000)
for name, g in (("normal", normal), ("heavy-tailed", heavy)):
    print(f"{name:12s}: theta = {np.quantile(g, 0.999) + 0.5:.2f} s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
normal      : theta = 1.69 s
heavy-tailed: theta = 2.89 s
```
::::
:::
::::

### Speed and accuracy of a heartbeat detector

A heartbeat detector has two knobs, $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ and $\theta$, and two qualities, how soon it notices a crash and how often it suspects a live node. The proposition makes the trade-off exact under
two assumptions: delays are bounded and losses are independent.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-heartbeat-detector}
#### Detection time and false suspicion of heartbeats

Let $p$ send heartbeats to $o$ every $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$, each delivered within a delay of at most $D$ or lost, losses independent with probability $q$, and let $o$ suspect $p$ after a silence of
$\theta$.

(a) (**Completeness**) If $p$ crashes at time $t$ and $o$ had received a heartbeat from it, $o$ suspects $p$ from some time no later than $t + D + \theta$ on, permanently.

(b) (**Accuracy**) If $p$ is alive and $\theta \geq k\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} + D$ for an integer $k \geq 1$, then $o$ suspects $p$ at a given time only if the $k$ heartbeats sent last before that time minus
$D$ were all lost; this has probability at most $q^k$.

(c) Over a period containing $H$ heartbeats, the expected number of times a suspicion of the live $p$ begins is at most $Hq^k$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) After $t$, $p$ sends nothing, so the last heartbeat $o$ receives arrives by $t + D$. From then on there is silence, so $o$ suspects $p$ by $t + D + \theta$ and, no heartbeat ever arriving, never
stops.

(b) Suppose $o$ suspects $p$ at time $\tau$: it received nothing in $(\tau - \theta, \tau]$. A heartbeat sent in $(\tau - \theta, \tau - D]$ would have arrived in that window unless lost, so all heartbeats
sent then were lost. That interval has length $\theta - D \geq k\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$, so it contains at least $k$ sending times, the last $k$ before $\tau - D$. By independence all are lost with probability
at most $q^k$.

(c) Each suspicion that begins is preceded by a run of at least $k$ consecutive lost heartbeats, ending at the onset, and two onsets are separated by a received heartbeat, so they belong to different
maximal runs. Assign each onset to the first heartbeat of its run; distinct onsets get distinct heartbeats. A run of at least $k$ losses begins at a given heartbeat with probability at most $q^k$, so by
linearity of expectation the number of onsets has mean at most $Hq^k$. $\square$

The trade-off is that $\theta$ enters both bounds: detection takes up to $D + \theta \geq k\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} + 2D$, and false suspicions fall like $q^k$. Halving $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ halves the detection
time at the same $k$, at twice the traffic. Both assumptions can fail: a process that pauses for longer than $\theta$ (a long garbage collection, a swapped-out machine) looks crashed although part (b)'s losses
did not happen, and losses on a congested link come in bursts.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A one-second heartbeat with a five-second timeout is a common setting. Part (a) gives its detection time.

::: {#exm-phd-default}
#### One second, five seconds

With $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} = 1\,\mathrm{s}$, $\theta = 5\,\mathrm{s}$ and $D = 0.1\,\mathrm{s}$, a crash is suspected within $5.1\,\mathrm{s}$, and $k = 4$ (since $4 + 0.1 \leq 5$), so with $q = 0.01$ a live node is
suspected at a given time with probability at most $10^{-8}$.
:::

Part (c) turns the bound into a rate. A day has many heartbeats.

::: {#exm-phd-per-day}
#### False suspicions per day

With one heartbeat per second, a day has $86\,400$; with $q = 0.01$, part (c) bounds the expected false suspicions per day by $0.086$ for $k = 3$ and $8.6 \times 10^{-4}$ for $k = 4$.

```{.python .run}
for k in (2, 3, 4):
    print(f"k = {k}: at most {86_400 * 0.01**k:.2e} false suspicions per day")
```

```{.text .run-output}
k = 2: at most 8.64e+00 false suspicions per day
k = 3: at most 8.64e-02 false suspicions per day
k = 4: at most 8.64e-04 false suspicions per day
```
:::

A table shows the trade-off. Detection time grows with $k$, false suspicions fall.

::: {#exm-phd-table}
#### The trade-off

For $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} = 0.5\,\mathrm{s}$, $D = 0.05\,\mathrm{s}$ and $q = 0.01$:

```{.python .run}
dhb, D, q = 0.5, 0.05, 0.01
for k in range(1, 6):
    theta = k * dhb + D
    print(f"k = {k}: theta {theta:.2f} s, detection <= {theta + D:.2f} s, false suspicions per day <= {86_400 / dhb * q**k:.2e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
k = 1: theta 0.55 s, detection <= 0.60 s, false suspicions per day <= 1.73e+03
k = 2: theta 1.05 s, detection <= 1.10 s, false suspicions per day <= 1.73e+01
k = 3: theta 1.55 s, detection <= 1.60 s, false suspicions per day <= 1.73e-01
k = 4: theta 2.05 s, detection <= 2.10 s, false suspicions per day <= 1.73e-03
k = 5: theta 2.55 s, detection <= 2.60 s, false suspicions per day <= 1.73e-05
```
:::

A simulation checks part (b). Suspicion is measured at random times.

::: {#exm-phd-simulation}
#### Simulated accuracy

With $q = 0.2$, $k = 3$ and random delays in $[0, D]$, the fraction of random times at which a live node is suspected stays below $0.2^3 = 0.008$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(37)
dhb, D, q, k = 1.0, 0.2, 0.2, 3
theta = k * dhb + D
send = np.arange(0, 10**5) * dhb
arr = np.sort((send + rng.uniform(0, D, send.size))[rng.random(send.size) > q])
probes = rng.uniform(100, send[-1], 10**5)
last = arr[np.searchsorted(arr, probes) - 1]
print(f"suspected at {np.mean(probes - last > theta):.4f} of probe times; bound {q**k}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
suspected at 0.0068 of probe times; bound 0.008000000000000002
```
:::

Liu's "couple of seconds" is part (a) plus an election. Detection dominates.

::: {#exm-phd-liu}
#### Seconds of downtime

Liu warns that a leader failover leaves the system "down for a couple of seconds or more because it takes time to determine a leader is down using timeouts" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5]. With
$\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} = 0.5\,\mathrm{s}$ and $k = 3$, part (a) alone gives up to $1.6\,\mathrm{s}$ before any election starts.
:::

Dynamo's detector uses client traffic as heartbeats. Its $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ is the gap between requests.

::: {#exm-phd-dynamo}
#### Requests as heartbeats

In Dynamo "a node A quickly discovers that a node B is unresponsive when B fails to respond to a message" [@decandia2007dynamo, Sec. 4.8.3, p. 213]: requests between A and B act as heartbeats, at the
request rate, so busy pairs detect quickly and idle pairs not at all, which Dynamo accepts since "in the absence of client requests ... neither node really needs to know".
:::

A long pause defeats part (b). The bounded-delay assumption fails.

::: {#exm-phd-pause}
#### A garbage-collection pause

A live process that stops for $8\,\mathrm{s}$ sends no heartbeats; with $\theta = 5\,\mathrm{s}$ it is suspected for $3\,\mathrm{s}$ although no heartbeat was lost. Part (b) assumes that heartbeats are sent
on time, and a paused process breaks that, which is why Bigtable makes a server that lost its lock stop serving (@exr-fd-bigtable-fence).
:::

Bigtable's master counts failed attempts. That is $k$ in part (b).

::: {#exm-phd-bigtable}
#### Several attempts

The master acts "if a tablet server reports that it has lost its lock, or if the master was unable to reach a server during its last several attempts" [@chang2006bigtable, Sec. 5.2, p. 4]. Requiring $k$
failed polls, each failing for a live server independently with probability $q$, is part (b) with polls as heartbeats: a live server is wrongly pursued with probability $q^k$ per check.
:::

Correlated losses change the bound. A burst loses many heartbeats at once.

::: {#exm-phd-burst}
#### Bursts

If losses come in bursts, for example a link that is down for $3\,\mathrm{s}$ with probability $10^{-4}$ per second, then $k = 3$ consecutive losses at $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} = 1\,\mathrm{s}$ happen with
probability about $10^{-4}$ per second, not $q^3$: the independence in part (b) matters more than $q$.
:::
