The proposition also prices the web stack's heartbeats. A WebSocket connection is a monitored node.

::: {#exm-phd-websocket}
#### Heartbeats on a connection

For the heartbeats of @def-real-time-delivery at $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} = 30\,\mathrm{s}$, a server that closes connections silent for $\theta = 65\,\mathrm{s}$ detects a dead client within about $65\,\mathrm{s}$
plus the delay, and with $k = 2$ and $q = 0.01$ closes a live one with probability at most $10^{-4}$ at a given moment.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise chooses $k$ for a target. Part (c) gives the inequality.

::: {#exr-phd-choose-k}
#### Choosing $k$

A cluster of $1000$ monitored nodes, each observed by one detector with $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} = 1\,\mathrm{s}$ and $q = 0.005$, should see at most one false suspicion a year in total. Find the smallest $k$
and the resulting detection time with $D = 0.1\,\mathrm{s}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A year of heartbeats from $1000$ nodes is $H = 3.15 \times 10^{10}$; part (c) needs $Hq^k \leq 1$, so $k \geq \ln H/\ln(1/q) = 4.6$, $k = 5$. Then $\theta = 5.1\,\mathrm{s}$ and detection takes up to
$5.2\,\mathrm{s}$.

## Python

The computation.

```{.python .run}
import math
H, q = 1000 * 365 * 86_400, 0.005
k = math.ceil(math.log(H) / math.log(1 / q))
print(f"k = {k}, expected false suspicions per year <= {H * q**k:.3f}, detection <= {k * 1 + 0.1 + 0.1:.1f} s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
k = 5, expected false suspicions per year <= 0.099, detection <= 5.2 s
```
::::
:::

The second exercise computes the mean detection time. A crash falls at a random point of the heartbeat cycle.

::: {#exr-phd-mean-detection}
#### Mean detection time

With no losses and a constant delay $D$, a crash at a uniform time within a heartbeat interval is suspected at $\theta$ after the last heartbeat's arrival. Prove that the mean detection time is
$\theta + D - \Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}/2$, and evaluate for the setting of @exm-phd-default.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If the last heartbeat before the crash was sent at $s$ and the crash is at $s + u$ with $u$ uniform on $[0, \Delta_{\mathrm{hb}})$, suspicion begins at $s + D + \theta$, so the detection time is $D + \theta - u$, with
mean $D + \theta - \Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}/2$: $4.6\,\mathrm{s}$ for the default setting.

## Python

A simulation of crash times.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
dhb, theta, D = 1.0, 5.0, 0.1
u = np.random.default_rng(38).uniform(0, dhb, 10**6)
print(f"mean detection {np.mean(D + theta - u):.3f} s, formula {theta + D - dhb / 2:.3f} s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean detection 4.601 s, formula 4.600 s
```
::::
:::

The third exercise shows that part (b) is tight. Exactly $k$ heartbeats can fit.

::: {#exr-phd-tight}
#### Tightness of part (b)

Show that with $\theta = k\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} + D$ and delays exactly $D$, the probability of suspicion just before a heartbeat arrives is exactly $q^k$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Just before the arrival of the heartbeat sent at $s$, the window $(\tau - \theta, \tau]$ contains the arrivals of exactly the $k$ previous heartbeats (sent at $s - \Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}, \dots, s - k\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$),
and the one sent at $s - (k+1)\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ arrives just outside it. Suspicion means those $k$ were lost: probability $q^k$.

## Python

A simulation at those instants.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(39)
q, k, T = 0.3, 2, 10**6
lost = rng.random(T) < q
runs = np.all([lost[k - j: T - j] for j in range(1, k + 1)], axis=0)
print(f"fraction of instants suspected {runs.mean():.4f}, q^k = {q**k:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
fraction of instants suspected 0.0905, q^k = 0.0900
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise simulates bursty losses. Part (b) underestimates them.

::: {#exr-phd-bursty}
#### A two-state link

A link alternates between a good state (loss $0.001$) and a bad state (loss $0.5$), moving from good to bad with probability $0.001$ per heartbeat and back with probability $0.2$. Compare the frequency of
three consecutive losses with $\bar q^3$, where $\bar q$ is the long-run loss rate.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The link is bad about $0.5\%$ of the time, so $\bar q \approx 0.0035$ and $\bar q^3 \approx 4 \times 10^{-8}$; but runs of three losses happen mostly inside bad periods, at a rate of a few times $10^{-4}$
per heartbeat, four orders of magnitude above $\bar q^3$. Independence fails, and the bound of part (b) is off by orders of magnitude.

## Python

The simulation.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(40)
T = 2 * 10**6; bad = np.zeros(T, bool); s = False; u = rng.random(T)
for i in range(T):
    s = (u[i] < 0.001) if not s else (u[i] >= 0.2); bad[i] = s
lost = rng.random(T) < np.where(bad, 0.5, 0.001)
run3 = np.mean(lost[2:] & lost[1:-1] & lost[:-2])
print(f"loss rate {lost.mean():.4f}, three in a row {run3:.2e}, independent prediction {lost.mean()**3:.2e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
loss rate 0.0036, three in a row 4.14e-04, independent prediction 4.51e-08
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise scales part (c) to a cluster. Many monitored pairs add up.

::: {#exr-phd-cluster}
#### All pairs

In a full mesh of $n$ nodes every node monitors every other. With $k = 3$, $q = 0.01$ and one heartbeat per second, how many false suspicions per day occur in total for $n = 100$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

There are $n(n - 1) = 9900$ monitored pairs, each with at most $86\,400 \times 10^{-6} = 0.086$ per day by part (c): up to $855$ false suspicions a day cluster-wide. Requiring two independent observers
(@exr-fd-two-sources) or a larger $k$ is needed at this scale.

## Python

The total.

```{.python .run}
n = 100
print(f"at most {n * (n - 1) * 86_400 * 0.01**3:.0f} false suspicions per day")
```

```{.text .run-output}
at most 855 false suspicions per day
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise asks what part (a) needs from the delay bound. Unbounded delays delay detection only.

::: {#exr-phd-unbounded}
#### Without a delay bound

Show that completeness (part (a)) does not need $D$ to be known, only that delays are finite, while accuracy (part (b)) fails for every $\theta$ if delays are unbounded.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

After a crash only finitely many heartbeats are in flight; each arrives at some finite time, and $\theta$ after the last of them $o$ suspects $p$ forever. For accuracy, if delays can exceed any bound, then for any
$\theta$ there is positive probability that $k$ consecutive heartbeats are each delayed by more than $\theta$, and $p$ is suspected while alive. No timeout makes a detector both complete and accurate when delays
are unbounded.

## Python

Exponential delays: the probability that a heartbeat takes longer than $\theta$ is positive for every $\theta$.

```{.python .run}
import math
for theta in (1, 5, 20):
    print(f"theta = {theta:2d} s: P(delay > theta) = {math.exp(-theta / 0.5):.2e} for exponential delays of mean 0.5 s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
theta =  1 s: P(delay > theta) = 1.35e-01 for exponential delays of mean 0.5 s
theta =  5 s: P(delay > theta) = 4.54e-05 for exponential delays of mean 0.5 s
theta = 20 s: P(delay > theta) = 4.25e-18 for exponential delays of mean 0.5 s
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise doubles the heartbeat rate. The proposition says what changes.

::: {#exr-phd-double}
#### Twice as many heartbeats

Starting from $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} = 1\,\mathrm{s}$, $k = 3$, halve $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$. Either keep $\theta$ (and double $k$) or keep $k$ (and halve $\theta$). Compare the detection times and false-suspicion
rates with $q = 0.01$, $D = 0.1\,\mathrm{s}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Keeping $\theta = 3.1\,\mathrm{s}$ gives $k = 6$: the same detection time and $q^6$ per heartbeat at twice the heartbeats, $2 \times 10^{-12}$ against $10^{-6}$ per second. Keeping $k = 3$ gives
$\theta = 1.6\,\mathrm{s}$: detection in $1.7\,\mathrm{s}$ instead of $3.2$, and twice the false-suspicion rate, $2 \times 10^{-6}$ per second. Faster heartbeats buy either accuracy or speed.

## Python

The three settings.

```{.python .run}
q, D = 0.01, 0.1
for dhb, k in ((1.0, 3), (0.5, 6), (0.5, 3)):
    theta = k * dhb + D
    print(f"dhb {dhb}, k {k}: detection <= {theta + D:.1f} s, false onsets per second <= {q**k / dhb:.1e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
dhb 1.0, k 3: detection <= 3.2 s, false onsets per second <= 1.0e-06
dhb 0.5, k 6: detection <= 3.2 s, false onsets per second <= 2.0e-12
dhb 0.5, k 3: detection <= 1.7 s, false onsets per second <= 2.0e-06
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise compares heartbeats with gossip-based detection. Gossip adds the spread time.

::: {#exr-phd-gossip-detection}
#### Detection through gossip

With gossip membership, a node learns that $p$'s counter stopped only after the last increase has spread to it. With $1000$ nodes gossiping once per second, compare the detection time with $T_{\mathrm{fail}} =
20\,\mathrm{s}$ against a direct heartbeat detector with $\theta = 5\,\mathrm{s}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The last increase reaches a node within the spread time, about $18$ rounds on average (@exm-fd-gossip-rounds), and the node marks $p$ failed $T_{\mathrm{fail}}$ after it saw that increase: between
$20$ and about $38\,\mathrm{s}$ after the crash. The direct detector takes about $5\,\mathrm{s}$ but needs $n(n-1)$ heartbeat streams; gossip is slower and far cheaper.

## Python

The range.

```{.python .run}
spread, tfail = 18, 20
print(f"gossip detection between {tfail} and about {tfail + spread} s; direct heartbeats about 5 s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
gossip detection between 20 and about 38 s; direct heartbeats about 5 s
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise proves part (c)'s assignment injective. The proof needs care with overlapping runs.

::: {#exr-phd-injective}
#### Onsets and runs

Prove that two distinct onsets of suspicion are assigned to different first heartbeats in the proof of part (c).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Between two onsets the suspicion must end, which requires a heartbeat to arrive, so some heartbeat between them was received. The run of losses before the later onset therefore begins after that received
heartbeat, and the run before the earlier onset ends before it: the runs are disjoint, and so are their first heartbeats.

## Python

Onsets and runs in a simulated loss sequence with $k = 2$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
lost = np.random.default_rng(41).random(10**5) < 0.3
k, onsets, starts, run = 2, 0, set(), 0
for i, x in enumerate(lost):
    run = run + 1 if x else 0
    if run == k:
        onsets += 1; starts.add(i - k + 1)
print("onsets", onsets, "| distinct run starts", len(starts))
```

```{.text .run-output}
onsets 6186 | distinct run starts 6186
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise sets the failure detector of the photo service's metadata leader. It combines this section with the first.

::: {#exr-phd-photo}
#### Detecting the metadata leader's failure

The metadata leader of @sec-leader-follower writes $2000$ entries per second with asynchronous replication. Choose $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ and $k$ for detection within $2\,\mathrm{s}$ and at most one false
failover a year with $q = 0.001$, $D = 0.05\,\mathrm{s}$, and estimate the writes rejected during a detection.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

One false failover a year needs $Hq^k \leq 1$ with $H = 3.15 \times 10^7/\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ heartbeats; detection needs $k\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} + 2D \leq 2$. With $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} = 0.25\,\mathrm{s}$, $H = 1.3 \times 10^8$ and
$k = 3$ gives $0.13$ per year and detection within $0.85\,\mathrm{s}$. During that time about $2000 \times 0.85 = 1700$ writes fail and must be retried.

## Python

A search over heartbeat intervals.

```{.python .run}
import math
q, D, year = 0.001, 0.05, 365 * 86_400
for dhb in (1.0, 0.5, 0.25):
    H = year / dhb; k = math.ceil(math.log(H) / math.log(1 / q)); det = k * dhb + 2 * D
    print(f"dhb {dhb}: k = {k}, false per year {H * q**k:.2f}, detection <= {det:.2f} s, writes failed ~ {2000 * det:.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
dhb 1.0: k = 3, false per year 0.03, detection <= 3.10 s, writes failed ~ 6200
dhb 0.5: k = 3, false per year 0.06, detection <= 1.60 s, writes failed ~ 3200
dhb 0.25: k = 3, false per year 0.13, detection <= 0.85 s, writes failed ~ 1700
```
::::
:::
::::

## Unique identifiers without coordination {#sec-unique-ids}

A single database hands out identifiers with an auto-increment counter. Once writes are spread over many nodes, that counter is either a bottleneck or a single point of
failure: "auto_increment does not work in a distributed environment because a single database server is not large enough and generating unique IDs across multiple databases
with minimal delay is challenging" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 7]. The alternatives either partition the space of identifiers among generators or make collisions so
unlikely that they can be ignored. Liu treats ID generators as tools: "you should be using the right generator for the correct use case" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5,
"ID Generator"]. This section defines the common schemes and bounds the probability that random identifiers collide.

For more on this topic, see @SystemDesignInterview2021 [Ch. 7], @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5, "ID Generator"] and @rfc9562 [Secs. 5.4, 5.7, 6.2, 6.4 and 6.11].

### Identifier schemes

The schemes differ in the coordination they need, the size of the identifier and whether identifiers sort by time. Xu's requirements for his design are a convenient test:
"IDs must be unique", "IDs are numerical values only", "IDs fit into 64-bit", "IDs are ordered by date", and the system must generate "over 10,000 unique IDs per second"
[@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 7, "Step 1"].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-unique-id}
#### Identifier schemes

1. An **auto-increment** identifier is the next value of a counter kept by one database. A **ticket server** is a database that does nothing but serve such values to many
   clients.
2. In **multi-master stride** allocation, $k$ servers each keep a counter; server $i$ issues $i, i + k, i + 2k, \dots$
3. A **UUID version 4** is a 128-bit value of which $122$ bits are random and $6$ fix the version and variant. A **UUID version 7** has a 48-bit Unix timestamp in milliseconds in its most
   significant bits, followed by the version, variant and $74$ bits that are random or a counter.
4. A **Snowflake** identifier is a 64-bit integer made of a sign bit $0$, a 41-bit timestamp in milliseconds since a chosen epoch, a 10-bit machine identifier (5 bits of data centre and
   5 of machine in Xu's layout) and a 12-bit **sequence number** that counts identifiers issued by the machine within the current millisecond.
5. A scheme is **coordination-free** if generators issue identifiers without exchanging messages after they have been assigned their parameters; an identifier is **time-ordered** if
   identifiers issued at later times compare greater.
:::

::::

Item 3 follows the standard: UUIDv4 "is meant for generating UUIDs from truly random or pseudorandom numbers", with "122 bits total" of random data, and UUIDv7 allocates "a Unix
timestamp in milliseconds in the most significant 48 bits" and fills "the remaining 74 bits, excluding the required version and variant bits, with random bits"
[@rfc9562, Secs. 5.4 and 5.7].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
SQLite's `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` is item 1. One database, one counter.

::: {#exm-id-auto}
#### Auto-increment

Each insert without an identifier receives the next integer, which is unique and ordered within the database, and needs every insert to pass through it.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE photos(photo_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, caption TEXT)")
for c in ("harbour", "market", "night"):
    db.execute("INSERT INTO photos(caption) VALUES (?)", (c,))
print(db.execute("SELECT * FROM photos").fetchall())
```

```{.text .run-output}
[(1, 'harbour'), (2, 'market'), (3, 'night')]
```
:::

Flickr's odd and even servers are item 2 with $k = 2$. Liu and Xu both describe it.

::: {#exm-id-stride}
#### Odd and even

"A famous example by Flickr is to have one server generate odd numbers, and the other server generates even numbers" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Auto Increment Multiple
Machines"]; Xu: "instead of increasing the next ID by 1, we increase it by k, where k is the number of database servers in use" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 7].

```{.python .run}
k = 2
servers = [iter(range(i, 20, k)) for i in (1, 2)]
print([next(servers[0]) for _ in range(5)], [next(servers[1]) for _ in range(5)])
```

```{.text .run-output}
[1, 3, 5, 7, 9] [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
```
:::

A UUIDv4 from Python's standard library shows the fixed bits. The version digit is $4$.

::: {#exm-id-uuid4}
#### A version 4 UUID

The thirteenth hex digit is the version and the seventeenth starts with the variant bits `10`, so it is one of `8`, `9`, `a`, `b`.

```{.python .run}
import uuid, random
u = uuid.UUID(int=random.Random(42).getrandbits(128), version=4)
print(u, "| version", u.version, "| variant digit", str(u)[19])
```

```{.text .run-output}
bdd640fb-0667-4ad1-9c80-317fa3b1799d | version 4 | variant digit 9
```
:::

Python 3.12 has no UUIDv7 function. The layout of item 3 builds one.

::: {#exm-id-uuid7}
#### A version 7 UUID

The run packs a fixed timestamp, the version $7$, the variant and random bits as in the standard's Figure 11, and shows that two identifiers a millisecond apart sort by time.

```{.python .run}
import uuid, random
rng = random.Random(7)
def uuid7(ms):
    value = (ms << 80) | (0x7 << 76) | (rng.getrandbits(12) << 64) | (0b10 << 62) | rng.getrandbits(62)
    return uuid.UUID(int=value)
a, b = uuid7(1_764_000_000_000), uuid7(1_764_000_000_001)
print(a, "| version", a.version); print(b, "| sorts after:", str(b) > str(a))
```

```{.text .run-output}
019ab697-e800-752e-89a7-834df2a74de4 | version 7
019ab697-e801-7651-8317-1ff4a6a3a450 | sorts after: True
```
:::

Snowflake packs four fields into 64 bits. Encoding and decoding are shifts.

::: {#exm-id-snowflake}
#### A Snowflake identifier

With Xu's layout and Twitter's "default epoch 1288834974657" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 7, "Twitter snowflake approach"], the run encodes data centre $3$, machine $17$ and sequence $5$
at a fixed time and decodes it.

```{.python .run}
EPOCH = 1288834974657
def encode(ms, dc, machine, seq):
    return ((ms - EPOCH) << 22) | (dc << 17) | (machine << 12) | seq
def decode(x):
    return (x >> 22) + EPOCH, (x >> 17) & 31, (x >> 12) & 31, x & 4095
x = encode(1_764_000_000_000, 3, 17, 5)
print(x, x.bit_length(), "bits |", decode(x))
```

```{.text .run-output}
1992986566456709125 61 bits | (1764000000000, 3, 17, 5)
```
:::

Xu's 41 bits of milliseconds last about 69 years. The epoch sets when they run out.

::: {#exm-id-69-years}
#### Sixty-nine years

"The maximum timestamp that can be represented in 41 bits is $2^{41} - 1 = 2199023255551$ milliseconds ... ~ 69 years", so "having a custom epoch time close to today's date delays the overflow
time" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 7]. From Twitter's epoch in November 2010 the field overflows in 2080.

```{.python .run}
import datetime
ms = 2**41 - 1
print(f"{ms / 1000 / 86400 / 365.25:.1f} years; overflow at",
      datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp((1288834974657 + ms) / 1000, datetime.timezone.utc).date())
```

```{.text .run-output}
69.7 years; overflow at 2080-07-10
```
:::

A ticket server is a single point of failure. Xu lists it as the main drawback.

::: {#exm-id-ticket}
#### A ticket server

The ticket server uses "a centralized auto_increment feature in a single database server"; it gives "numeric IDs" and is "easy to implement", but "if the ticket server goes down, all
systems that depend on it will face issues", and multiple ticket servers "introduce new challenges such as data synchronization" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 7, "Ticket Server"]. Two
ticket servers with stride $2$ are item 2.
:::

Liu uses ZooKeeper's transaction counter for strongly ordered identifiers. It costs a consensus round.

::: {#exm-id-zookeeper}
#### A consistent counter

A "strongly consistent (linearizable) system like ZooKeeper can generate guaranteed monotonically increasing integer numbers using zxid"; the cost is that "due to the leader-follower quorum to
guarantee strongly consistent ordering, the throughput is lower", and its uses include "Snowflake machine ID generation when initially booted" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5].
:::

Time-ordered identifiers make index inserts local. The standard explains why.

::: {#exm-id-locality}
#### Index locality

"Time-ordered monotonic UUIDs benefit from greater database-index locality because the new values are near each other in the index", and "the real-world differences in this approach of index
locality versus random data inserts can be one order of magnitude or more" [@rfc9562, Sec. 6.11]. In a B-tree (@def-storage-engine) a random key lands on a random leaf, a time-ordered key on the
rightmost one.
:::

Xu's comparison table summarises the trade-offs. Only Snowflake meets all five requirements.

::: {#exm-id-xu-choice}
#### Choosing a scheme

Multi-master stride is "hard to scale with multiple data centers" and its IDs "do not go up with time across multiple servers"; UUIDs are "128 bits long, but our requirement is 64 bits" and "do not go
up with time"; the ticket server is a "single point of failure"; Xu settles on Snowflake "as it supports all our use cases and is scalable in a distributed environment" [@SystemDesignInterview2021,
Ch. 7].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise proves that stride allocation never collides. Residues separate the servers.

::: {#exr-id-stride-unique}
#### Strides are disjoint

Prove that the $k$ servers of item 2 never issue the same identifier, and show what goes wrong if a third server is added to two servers without reconfiguring them, as Liu warns: "Imagine adding a
third machine; you would need to reconfigure the servers to generate in multiples of 3" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Server $i$ issues only numbers congruent to $i$ modulo $k$, and distinct $i \in \{1, \dots, k\}$ have distinct residues, so the sets are disjoint. A third server with stride $3$ beside two servers with
stride $2$ issues $3, 6, 9, \dots$, and $6$ is also even, issued by server 2: the residue classes of different moduli overlap.

## Python

The collision.

```{.python .run}
odd, even, third = set(range(1, 30, 2)), set(range(2, 30, 2)), set(range(3, 30, 3))
print("odd & even:", odd & even, "| third & even:", sorted(third & even), "| third & odd:", sorted(third & odd))
```

```{.text .run-output}
odd & even: set() | third & even: [6, 12, 18, 24] | third & odd: [3, 9, 15, 21, 27]
```
::::
:::

The second exercise checks Xu's figure for UUIDs. The birthday bound decides.

::: {#exr-id-xu-uuid}
#### One billion a second for a century

Xu quotes that "after generating 1 billion UUIDs every second for approximately 100 years would the probability of creating a single duplicate reach 50%" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 7]. Each pair of $n$
UUIDv4s is equal with probability $2^{-122}$, so the expected number of equal pairs is $\binom n2 2^{-122}$; treating that number as
[Poisson](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#thm-poisson-limit), find the number of years at which the probability of at least one reaches $1/2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With a Poisson number of equal pairs of mean $\mu = n^2/2^{123}$, the probability of none is $e^{-\mu}$, which is $1/2$ at $\mu = \ln 2$, that is $n = \sqrt{2^{123}\ln 2} = 2.7 \times 10^{18}$. At $10^9$ per second that takes
$2.7 \times 10^9\,\mathrm{s}$, about $86$ years: Xu's "approximately 100 years" is the right order.

## Python

The computation.

```{.python .run}
import math
n = math.sqrt(2**123 * math.log(2))
print(f"n = {n:.2e}, years at 1e9 per second: {n / 1e9 / (365.25 * 86_400):.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
n = 2.71e+18, years at 1e9 per second: 86
```
::::
:::

The third exercise measures Snowflake's throughput. Twelve bits per millisecond per machine.

::: {#exr-id-snowflake-rate}
#### How many per second

Find the maximum identifiers per second of one Snowflake machine and of the whole layout, compare with Xu's requirement of $10^4$ per second, and say what a machine must do when its sequence is
exhausted within a millisecond.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$4096$ per millisecond is $4.1 \times 10^6$ per second per machine, and $1024$ machines give $4.2 \times 10^9$: far above $10^4$. A machine that has issued $4096$ in one millisecond must wait for the next
millisecond before issuing more, or it would repeat a sequence number.

## Python

The rates.

```{.python .run}
print(f"per machine {4096 * 1000:.2e}/s, all machines {4096 * 1000 * 1024:.2e}/s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
per machine 4.10e+06/s, all machines 4.19e+09/s
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise breaks Snowflake with a clock that goes back. The sequence restarts on a reused millisecond.

::: {#exr-id-clock-back}
#### A clock that goes backwards

A Snowflake generator resets its sequence to $0$ whenever the millisecond changes. Its clock is stepped back by $5\,\mathrm{ms}$ by a time synchronisation. Show that it can issue a duplicate, and fix it by
remembering the last timestamp used.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

After the step, the generator sees milliseconds it has already used and restarts their sequence at $0$, issuing identifiers it issued $5\,\mathrm{ms}$ earlier. Keeping the last timestamp and refusing (or
waiting) while the clock reads less, or using $\max(\text{clock}, \text{last})$, restores uniqueness, at the price of IDs that run ahead of the clock for a while. Xu flags clock synchronisation as an open issue
(Ch. 7, "Step 4").

## Python

The naive and the guarded generator under the same clock readings.

```{.python .run}
clock = [100, 100, 101, 102, 97, 98, 100, 101]                      # stepped back after 102
def gen(guard):
    last, seq, out = -1, 0, []
    for t in clock:
        if guard: t = max(t, last)
        seq = seq + 1 if t == last else 0
        last = t; out.append((t, seq))
    return out
for g in (False, True):
    ids = gen(g)
    print("guarded" if g else "naive  ", ids, "| duplicates:", len(ids) - len(set(ids)))
```

```{.text .run-output}
naive   [(100, 0), (100, 1), (101, 0), (102, 0), (97, 0), (98, 0), (100, 0), (101, 0)] | duplicates: 2
guarded [(100, 0), (100, 1), (101, 0), (102, 0), (102, 1), (102, 2), (102, 3), (102, 4)] | duplicates: 0
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise inserts random and time-ordered keys into a B-tree. The pages written show the locality of @exm-id-locality.

::: {#exr-id-btree}
#### Random against ordered keys

Model a B-tree index as leaves of $100$ keys in key order. Insert $2 \times 10^4$ keys in random and in increasing order, and count the distinct leaves touched by the last $1000$ inserts of each.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

An insert touches the leaf that holds its rank among the keys present. Increasing keys always rank last, so they fill one leaf after another: $1000$ inserts touch $10$ leaves, each many times in a row while it is
in memory. Random keys rank uniformly, so $1000$ inserts touch nearly all of the $200$ leaves, in no order, each a likely cache miss: the locality behind the standard's "one order of magnitude".

## Python

The leaves touched, from the ranks of the inserted keys.

```{.python .run}
import random, bisect
random.seed(42)
keys = random.sample(range(10**12), 20_000)
for name, order in (("random", keys), ("increasing", sorted(keys))):
    present, touched = [], set()
    for i, k in enumerate(order):
        r = bisect.bisect_left(present, k); present.insert(r, k)
        if i >= len(order) - 1000:
            touched.add(r // 100)
    print(f"{name:10s}: distinct leaves touched by the last 1000 inserts: {len(touched)}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
random    : distinct leaves touched by the last 1000 inserts: 195
increasing: distinct leaves touched by the last 1000 inserts: 10
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise compares the two Snowflake layouts. Liu and Xu split the 10 bits differently.

::: {#exr-id-machine-bits}
#### Ten machine bits

Liu's Snowflake has a 10-bit machine identifier "assigned by ZooKeeper during machine bootup", giving "up to 1024 machines" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5]; Xu splits the same bits into $5$ of data
centre and $5$ of machine. When does each fit better, and how many machines can a single data centre have in each?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Both allow $1024$ generators. Xu's split fixes at most $32$ per data centre and $32$ data centres, which suits a few large regions assigned statically; Liu's flat field lets one data centre use all
$1024$, at the price of a coordination service to hand out identifiers without repeats.

## Python

The limits.

```{.python .run}
print(f"Xu: {2**5} data centres x {2**5} machines; Liu: {2**10} machines anywhere")
```

```{.text .run-output}
Xu: 32 data centres x 32 machines; Liu: 1024 machines anywhere
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise estimates how often Snowflake identifiers from two machines are out of time order. Clock skew decides.

::: {#exr-id-skew}
#### Roughly sorted

Liu notes that Snowflake is "still not perfectly ordered. If two different machines generate two IDs, it's unclear who was generated first" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5]. Two machines' clocks
differ by a skew uniform in $[-5, 5]\,\mathrm{ms}$, and IDs are issued at random times $1\,\mathrm{ms}$ apart on average. Estimate the fraction of consecutive pairs from different machines that are out of order.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A pair issued $g$ apart in real time is inverted when the skew exceeds $g$ in the wrong direction. With exponential gaps of mean $1\,\mathrm{ms}$ and skew uniform on $[-5, 5]$, the probability is the mean of
$\mathbb P(\text{skew} > g)$, about $0.4$: identifiers from different machines are ordered only to within the skew.

## Python

A simulation.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(43)
g = rng.exponential(1.0, 10**6); skew = rng.uniform(-5, 5, 10**6)
print(f"fraction out of order: {np.mean(skew > g):.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
fraction out of order: 0.401
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise computes the collision risk of UUIDv7 within a millisecond. Only identifiers of the same millisecond can collide.

::: {#exr-id-uuid7-collision}
#### Collisions in one millisecond

UUIDv7 identifiers that share a millisecond differ only in their $74$ random bits. If a service issues $10^6$ per millisecond, bound the probability of a collision within one millisecond and over a year.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Within one millisecond each of the $\binom n2$ pairs is equal with probability $2^{-74}$, so by the union bound of the
[rules of probability](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#prp-probability-rules) a collision has probability at most $n^2/2^{75} = 2.6 \times 10^{-11}$; over $3.15 \times 10^{10}$
milliseconds of a year, by the union bound again, at most $0.83$. At this extreme rate UUIDv7's random bits are not enough, which is why the standard allows a counter in them [@rfc9562, Sec. 6.2].

## Python

The two bounds.

```{.python .run}
p = (1e6)**2 / 2**75
print(f"per millisecond <= {p:.2e}; per year <= {p * 365 * 86_400 * 1000:.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
per millisecond <= 2.65e-11; per year <= 0.83
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise designs a photo identifier. It combines this section with partitioning.

::: {#exr-id-photo}
#### An identifier for photos

Design a 64-bit photo identifier that is time-ordered, issued without coordination by up to $512$ upload servers, and carries the owner's partition among $1024$, so that a photo can be found without an index
(@def-request-routing). Allocate the bits and give the throughput.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Sign $1$, timestamp $41$ (milliseconds, 69 years), partition $10$, server $9$, leaving $3$ bits of sequence: $8$ photos per millisecond per server, $4 \times 10^6$ per second in total, far above the
$2 \times 10^7$ uploads a day ($230$ per second). The partition field lets the router send `get(photo_id)` to the right partition directly.

## Python

The layout checked for $64$ bits and the throughput.

```{.python .run}
bits = {"sign": 1, "time": 41, "partition": 10, "server": 9, "seq": 3}
print(sum(bits.values()), "bits; per second", 2**bits["seq"] * 1000 * 2**bits["server"], "| needed", round(2e7 / 86_400))
```

```{.text .run-output}
64 bits; per second 4096000 | needed 231
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise asks which schemes are coordination-free. Item 5 decides.

::: {#exr-id-classify}
#### Which need coordination

Classify auto-increment, ticket server, stride, UUIDv4, UUIDv7 and Snowflake as coordination-free or not, and as time-ordered or not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Auto-increment and the ticket server need every request to reach one server: not coordination-free, ordered. Stride is coordination-free after the residues are assigned, but not time-ordered across servers.
UUIDv4 is coordination-free and unordered. UUIDv7 and Snowflake are coordination-free (Snowflake after machine identifiers are assigned) and time-ordered up to clock skew.

## Python

The table.

```{.python .run}
rows = [("auto-increment", "no", "yes"), ("ticket server", "no", "yes"), ("stride", "yes", "no"), ("UUIDv4", "yes", "no"),
        ("UUIDv7", "yes", "up to skew"), ("Snowflake", "yes", "up to skew")]
for name, free, ordered in rows:
    print(f"{name:15s} coordination-free: {free:4s} time-ordered: {ordered}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
auto-increment  coordination-free: no   time-ordered: yes
ticket server   coordination-free: no   time-ordered: yes
stride          coordination-free: yes  time-ordered: no
UUIDv4          coordination-free: yes  time-ordered: no
UUIDv7          coordination-free: yes  time-ordered: up to skew
Snowflake       coordination-free: yes  time-ordered: up to skew
```
::::
:::
::::

### Collisions of random identifiers

Random identifiers are unique only with high probability. The birthday problem gives the probability exactly, and two inequalities bracket it in a form that can be inverted.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-id-collision}
#### Collisions of random identifiers

Let $n$ identifiers be drawn independently and uniformly from $N_b = 2^b$ values, with $n \leq N_b$.

(a) The probability $P_{\mathrm{col}}$ that two of them are equal satisfies
$$
1 - e^{-n(n-1)/(2N_b)} \;\leq\; P_{\mathrm{col}} \;\leq\; \frac{n(n-1)}{2N_b}.
$$

(b) $P_{\mathrm{col}} \leq \varepsilon$ holds whenever $n(n - 1) \leq 2\varepsilon N_b$, and $P_{\mathrm{col}} \geq 1/2$ whenever $n(n-1) \geq 2\ln 2\,N_b$; so about $\sqrt{N_b} = 2^{b/2}$ identifiers make a
collision likely.

(c) Identifiers made of a generator field, unique per generator, and a value that the generator never repeats, never collide.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) The $i$-th identifier, for $i = 2, \dots, n$, differs from the previous $i - 1$ (themselves distinct) with probability $1 - (i - 1)/N_b$, so
$$
1 - P_{\mathrm{col}} = \prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\Big(1 - \frac{i}{N_b}\Big) \leq \prod_{i=1}^{n-1}e^{-i/N_b} = e^{-n(n-1)/(2N_b)},
$$
using $1 - x \leq e^{-x}$, which gives the lower bound. For the upper bound, a collision means that some pair is equal; each of the $\binom n2$ pairs is equal with probability $1/N_b$, and the union bound of
the [rules of probability](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#prp-probability-rules) gives $P_{\mathrm{col}} \leq \binom n2/N_b$.

(b) The first statement is the upper bound of (a). For the second, the lower bound of (a) is at least $1 - e^{-\ln 2} = 1/2$ when $n(n-1)/(2N_b) \geq \ln 2$.

(c) Two identifiers from different generators differ in the generator field; two from the same generator differ in the value. $\square$

Part (c) is the guarantee of stride allocation, Snowflake (machine identifier and a timestamp-and-sequence pair that the machine never repeats, given the clock guard of @exr-id-clock-back) and UUIDv7 with a
counter; parts (a) and (b) are the guarantee of UUIDv4 and of the random bits of UUIDv7, which the standard describes as entropy "sufficient to ensure that the chances of collision are low"
[@rfc9562, Sec. 6.4].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The bounds for UUIDv4 at the photo service's scale are tiny. Five years of photos are $3.65 \times 10^{10}$.

::: {#exm-ic-photos}
#### Photos with UUIDv4 identifiers

With $n = 3.65 \times 10^{10}$ and $b = 122$, part (a) bounds the collision probability by $n^2/2^{123} = 1.3 \times 10^{-16}$.

```{.python .run}
n = 3.65e10
print(f"{n * (n - 1) / 2**123:.2e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
1.25e-16
```
:::

Random 64-bit identifiers are a different matter. Part (b) puts the danger near four billion.

::: {#exm-ic-64bit}
#### Random 64-bit identifiers

For $b = 64$, $\sqrt{2\ln 2 \cdot 2^{64}} = 5.1 \times 10^9$ identifiers give a collision with probability at least $1/2$: random 64-bit IDs are unsafe for the photo service, which is why Snowflake structures its
64 bits instead.

```{.python .run}
import math
print(f"{math.sqrt(2 * math.log(2) * 2**64):.2e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
5.06e+09
```
:::

The bounds of part (a) are close for small probabilities. They differ when collisions are likely.

::: {#exm-ic-bracket}
#### How tight the bracket is

For $b = 32$: with $n = 10^3$ both bounds are about $1.16 \times 10^{-4}$; with $n = 10^5$ the upper bound exceeds $1$ while the lower is $0.69$, and the exact value is in between.

```{.python .run}
import math
N = 2**32
for n in (10**3, 10**5):
    exact = 1 - math.exp(sum(math.log1p(-i / N) for i in range(1, n)))
    print(f"n = {n}: lower {1 - math.exp(-n * (n - 1) / (2 * N)):.5f}, exact {exact:.5f}, upper {n * (n - 1) / (2 * N):.5f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
n = 1000: lower 0.00012, exact 0.00012, upper 0.00012
n = 100000: lower 0.68781, exact 0.68781, upper 1.16414
```
:::

A simulation confirms part (a) at a small size. Sixteen bits collide quickly.

::: {#exm-ic-simulation}
#### Collisions of 16-bit identifiers

With $b = 16$ and $n = 300$, part (a) gives $0.495 \leq P_{\mathrm{col}} \leq 0.684$; drawing $10^4$ samples gives a frequency inside the bracket.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(44)
hits = sum(len(np.unique(rng.integers(0, 2**16, 300))) < 300 for _ in range(10_000))
n, N = 300, 2**16
print(f"frequency {hits / 1e4:.3f}, bracket [{1 - np.exp(-n * (n - 1) / (2 * N)):.3f}, {n * (n - 1) / (2 * N):.3f}]")
```

```{.text .run-output}
frequency 0.501, bracket [0.496, 0.684]
```
:::

Part (c) covers Snowflake. Uniqueness is structural.

::: {#exm-ic-snowflake}
#### Snowflake by structure

Two Snowflake identifiers from different machines differ in the machine field; from the same machine, the pair (timestamp, sequence) is never repeated if the clock is guarded and the sequence waits at
$4096$. Part (c) gives uniqueness with probability one, not with high probability.
:::

Part (c) also covers stride allocation. The residue is the generator field.

::: {#exm-ic-stride}
#### Stride as structure

In stride allocation the residue modulo $k$ plays the generator field and the quotient the never-repeated value, so part (c) is @exr-id-stride-unique.
:::

UUIDv7 mixes the two mechanisms. Time separates milliseconds, randomness the rest.

::: {#exm-ic-uuid7}
#### UUIDv7

Identifiers from different milliseconds differ in the timestamp field; within one millisecond, part (a) applies to the $74$ random bits. At $10^3$ identifiers per millisecond the per-millisecond bound is
$10^6/2^{75} = 2.6 \times 10^{-17}$.
:::

Part (b) gives a rule of thumb. Halve the bits.

::: {#exm-ic-half-bits}
#### Half the bits

Part (b) says that $b$ random bits are safe for about $2^{b/2}$ identifiers, with a margin: for a collision probability of $10^{-9}$ the budget is $n \approx \sqrt{2 \cdot 10^{-9} \cdot 2^b}$, so $b = 122$
allows $1.0 \times 10^{14}$ identifiers and $b = 64$ only $1.9 \times 10^5$.

```{.python .run}
import math
for b in (64, 122):
    print(f"b = {b}: n = {math.sqrt(2e-9 * 2**b):.1e} for P <= 1e-9")
```

```{.text .run-output}
b = 64: n = 1.9e+05 for P <= 1e-9
b = 122: n = 1.0e+14 for P <= 1e-9
```
:::

The standard notes that more generators mean more risk. Part (a) says what matters is the total count.

::: {#exm-ic-rfc-nodes}
#### More generators

RFC 9562 warns that "as the total number of UUID generating nodes increases, so does the likelihood of a collision" [@rfc9562, Sec. 6.4]. For random identifiers part (a) depends only on the total $n$ of
identifiers drawn, so $100$ generators issuing $10^9$ each are exactly as safe as one generator issuing $10^{11}$; more nodes matter because they usually mean more identifiers, or weaker random sources.
:::

Hashes used as identifiers obey the same bound. A content hash is a random-looking value.

::: {#exm-ic-hash}
#### Content hashes

Object keys formed from the first $64$ bits of a SHA-256 of a photo's bytes behave like random identifiers for distinct photos, so part (b) applies: they collide with probability $1/2$ near $5 \times 10^9$
distinct photos, and need more bits for the $3.65 \times 10^{10}$ the service stores.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise inverts part (b) for a target probability. It sizes identifiers.

::: {#exr-ic-size}
#### How many bits

Find the smallest $b$ such that $10^{12}$ random identifiers collide with probability at most $10^{-6}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Part (b) needs $2^b \geq n(n - 1)/(2\varepsilon) \approx 5 \times 10^{29}$, so $b \geq 98.6$: $99$ random bits. UUIDv4's $122$ suffice with room.

## Python

The computation.

```{.python .run}
import math
n, eps = 1e12, 1e-6
print(f"b >= {math.log2(n * (n - 1) / (2 * eps)):.1f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
b >= 98.7
```
::::
:::

The second exercise computes the exact collision probability by recursion. It checks the bracket.

::: {#exr-ic-exact}
#### The exact probability

Compute $P_{\mathrm{col}}$ exactly from the product in the proof for $b = 20$ and $n = 500, 1000, 2000$, and check it against both bounds.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The product $\prod(1 - i/N_b)$ is computed in logarithms to avoid underflow. Each exact value lies between the two bounds, as part (a) proves.

## Python

The three cases.

```{.python .run}
import math
N = 2**20
for n in (500, 1000, 2000):
    exact = 1 - math.exp(sum(math.log1p(-i / N) for i in range(1, n)))
    lo, hi = 1 - math.exp(-n * (n - 1) / (2 * N)), n * (n - 1) / (2 * N)
    print(f"n = {n}: {lo:.4f} <= {exact:.4f} <= {hi:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
n = 500: 0.1122 <= 0.1122 <= 0.1190
n = 1000: 0.3790 <= 0.3791 <= 0.4764
n = 2000: 0.8514 <= 0.8516 <= 1.9064
```
::::
:::

The third exercise estimates the expected number of colliding pairs. It is the upper bound's quantity.

::: {#exr-ic-expected-pairs}
#### Expected colliding pairs

Prove that the expected number of equal pairs among $n$ random identifiers is exactly $\binom n2/N_b$, and explain why the upper bound of part (a) is this expectation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Each pair is equal with probability $1/N_b$, and by linearity of [expectation](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#def-expectation) the number of equal pairs has mean $\binom n2/N_b$.
The probability of at least one equal pair is at most the expected number, by Markov's inequality for a non-negative integer variable, which is the upper bound.

## Python

A simulation with $b = 12$, $n = 50$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from math import comb
rng = np.random.default_rng(45)
pairs = []
for _ in range(20_000):
    _, c = np.unique(rng.integers(0, 2**12, 50), return_counts=True)
    pairs.append(sum(comb(int(x), 2) for x in c))
print(f"mean equal pairs {np.mean(pairs):.4f}, formula {comb(50, 2) / 2**12:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean equal pairs 0.3028, formula 0.2991
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise mixes structure and randomness. A generator field shrinks the random problem.

::: {#exr-ic-mixed}
#### A generator field plus random bits

$1000$ generators each issue $10^9$ identifiers made of a 10-bit generator field and $54$ random bits. Bound the collision probability, and compare with $64$ random bits for the same $10^{12}$ identifiers.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Identifiers from different generators never collide (part (c)), but within one generator the upper bound of part (a) is $(10^9)^2/2^{55} \approx 28$, useless, and by part (b) collisions are likely beyond
about $2^{27} \approx 1.3 \times 10^8$ identifiers per generator: $54$ random bits are far too few for $10^9$. Pure random $64$ bits fare no better, with a bound of $2.7 \times 10^4$. Structure removes
collisions between generators, but the random part must still be large for the identifiers that share a prefix.

## Python

Both bounds.

```{.python .run}
per_gen = (1e9)**2 / 2**55
print(f"per generator {per_gen:.3f}, all generators <= {1000 * per_gen:.1f}; pure random 64 bits <= {(1e12)**2 / 2**65:.1e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
per generator 27.756, all generators <= 27755.6; pure random 64 bits <= 2.7e+04
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise derives the square-root rule from part (a). The constant is $\sqrt{2\ln 2}$.

::: {#exr-ic-median}
#### Half the time

Prove that the number of random identifiers at which a collision first occurs has median between about $\sqrt{N_b}$ and $\sqrt{2\ln 2\,N_b} + 1$, using part (a).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The median $n^*$ is the first $n$ with $P_{\mathrm{col}}(n) \geq 1/2$. By part (b) $P_{\mathrm{col}} \geq 1/2$ once $n(n - 1) \geq 2\ln 2\,N_b$, so $n^* \leq \sqrt{2\ln 2\,N_b} + 1$. By the upper bound of part
(a), $P_{\mathrm{col}} < 1/2$ while $n(n - 1) < N_b$, so $n^* \geq \sqrt{N_b}$ roughly. The constants $\sqrt{2\ln 2} = 1.18$ and $1$ bracket the median within $18\%$; the median is near $1.18\sqrt{N_b}$.

## Python

The median for $b = 20$ by exact computation.

```{.python .run}
import math
N = 2**20; log_ok = 0.0; n = 1
while 1 - math.exp(log_ok) < 0.5:
    log_ok += math.log1p(-n / N); n += 1
print(f"median {n}, sqrt(N) = {math.sqrt(N):.0f}, sqrt(2 ln 2 N) = {math.sqrt(2 * math.log(2) * N):.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
median 1206, sqrt(N) = 1024, sqrt(2 ln 2 N) = 1206
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise asks how often a stride-free UUIDv4 table must check for duplicates. A unique index does it for free.

::: {#exr-ic-unique-index}
#### Checking anyway

A table keyed by UUIDv4 has a `PRIMARY KEY`. How many duplicate-key errors should be expected over five years of photo uploads, and what should the application do on one?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By @exm-ic-photos, the expected number is at most $1.3 \times 10^{-16}$: none. The key constraint still catches a collision caused by a bad random generator, and the right response is to draw a new
identifier and retry; the standard's warning that implementations should "weigh the consequences of UUID collisions" is about such failures of randomness [@rfc9562, Sec. 6.7].

## Python

A retry loop against a key constraint.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3, uuid, random
rng = random.Random(46)
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:"); db.execute("CREATE TABLE photos(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY)")
def insert():
    for attempt in range(3):
        try:
            db.execute("INSERT INTO photos VALUES (?)", (str(uuid.UUID(int=rng.getrandbits(128), version=4)),)); return attempt + 1
        except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
            continue
print("attempts for 1000 inserts:", sum(insert() for _ in range(1000)))
```

```{.text .run-output}
attempts for 1000 inserts: 1000
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise applies part (a) to short URLs. Seven base-62 characters are about 42 bits.

::: {#exr-ic-short-url}
#### Short codes

A link shortener draws random codes of $7$ characters from $62$ symbols. Find the number of codes at which a collision becomes likely, and what a generator must do instead at $10^9$ codes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$N_b = 62^7 = 3.5 \times 10^{12}$, so collisions are likely beyond about $\sqrt{2\ln 2 \cdot N_b} = 2.2 \times 10^6$ codes. At $10^9$ codes the generator must check for existing codes and redraw, or derive codes
from a unique counter (part (c)) encoded in base $62$.

## Python

The threshold.

```{.python .run}
import math
N = 62**7
print(f"N = {N:.2e}, likely collision after {math.sqrt(2 * math.log(2) * N):.2e} codes")
```

```{.text .run-output}
N = 3.52e+12, likely collision after 2.21e+06 codes
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise proves part (c) for Snowflake under the clock guard. It needs the sequence rule.

::: {#exr-ic-snowflake-proof}
#### Snowflake is unique

Prove that a Snowflake machine using $t = \max(\text{clock}, \text{last})$ and waiting for the next millisecond when its sequence would exceed $4095$ never issues the same (timestamp, sequence) pair twice.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The timestamps used never decrease, by the maximum. Within one timestamp the sequence increases from $0$ and never exceeds $4095$, because the machine waits; when the timestamp increases the pair differs in its
first entry. So pairs are strictly increasing in lexicographic order and never repeat; with distinct machine identifiers, part (c) gives uniqueness across machines.

## Python

The guarded generator under a backward clock and a burst.

```{.python .run}
def snow(clock, limit=4):
    last, seq, out = -1, 0, []
    for t in clock:
        t = max(t, last)
        if t == last:
            seq += 1
            if seq == limit:
                t, seq = last + 1, 0                     # wait for the next millisecond
        else:
            seq = 0
        last = t; out.append((t, seq))
    return out
ids = snow([5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 3, 3, 6])
print(ids, "| strictly increasing:", all(a < b for a, b in zip(ids, ids[1:])))
```

```{.text .run-output}
[(5, 0), (5, 1), (5, 2), (5, 3), (6, 0), (6, 1), (6, 2), (6, 3), (7, 0)] | strictly increasing: True
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise counts what a 122-bit identifier space allows per person. It is very large.

::: {#exr-ic-per-person}
#### Per person

If each of $10^{10}$ people generated $10^{6}$ UUIDv4 identifiers a day for $100$ years, bound the collision probability.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$n = 10^{10} \cdot 10^6 \cdot 36\,525 = 3.7 \times 10^{20}$, and $n^2/2^{123} = 1.3 \times 10^4$: a collision is then certain. UUIDv4 is safe for any single system's lifetime, not for an unbounded universe of
identifiers.

## Python

The bound.

```{.python .run}
n = 1e10 * 1e6 * 36_525
print(f"n = {n:.1e}, n^2 / 2^123 = {n * n / 2**123:.1e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
n = 3.7e+20, n^2 / 2^123 = 1.3e+04
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise compares the bounds of part (a) at Xu's rate. One billion a second.

::: {#exr-ic-xu-rate}
#### A year at a billion a second

At $10^9$ UUIDv4 identifiers per second, compute both bounds of part (a) after one year and after $50$ years.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

After a year $n = 3.2 \times 10^{16}$ and $n^2/2^{123} = 9.4 \times 10^{-5}$, with the lower bound essentially equal. After $50$ years $n = 1.6 \times 10^{18}$, the upper bound is $0.23$ and the lower $0.21$:
consistent with @exr-id-xu-uuid, where the probability reaches $1/2$ near $86$ years.

## Python

The bounds.

```{.python .run}
import math
for years in (1, 50):
    n = 1e9 * 365.25 * 86_400 * years; x = n * n / 2**123
    print(f"{years:2d} years: lower {1 - math.exp(-x):.2e}, upper {x:.2e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
 1 years: lower 9.36e-05, upper 9.37e-05
50 years: lower 2.09e-01, upper 2.34e-01
```
::::
:::
::::

## Exercises {#sec-replication-and-partitioning-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The three integrative exercises below combine the sections of the chapter. The first sizes the photo service's metadata cluster.

::: {#exr-replication-and-partitioning-int-1}
#### Sizing the metadata cluster

The photo metadata, $36.5\,\mathrm{TB}$ after five years, is partitioned by consistent hashing over $n$ nodes of $2\,\mathrm{TB}$ usable each, with $N = 3$ replicas and $(R, W) = (2, 2)$. (a) Find $n$ so that the
busiest node is under $80\%$ full, using @thm-consistent-hashing (d) with $v = 256$ and a margin of three standard deviations. (b) Find the read and write availability with replicas up independently with
probability $0.995$ (@thm-quorum-intersection, @prp-series-parallel-availability). (c) Estimate the keys moved when one node is added.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

(a) Each node holds $3 \times 36.5/n\,\mathrm{TB}$ on average, and with $v = 256$ the relative standard deviation is about $1/16$, so the busiest node holds about $(1 + 3/16)$ times the mean. The condition
$1.19 \times 109.5/n \leq 1.6$ gives $n \geq 82$. (b) Reads and writes each need two of three replicas: $1 - 3 \cdot 0.005^2 \cdot 0.995 - 0.005^3 = 0.999925$. (c) By part (b) of the theorem a new node takes
$1/(n + 1)$ of the key space, about $0.44\,\mathrm{TB}$ of primary data and three times that with replicas.

## Python

The three parts.

```{.python .run}
import math
total, cap, v = 3 * 36.5, 2.0, 256
for n in range(60, 120):
    sd = math.sqrt((n - 1) / (n * v + 1))
    if (1 + 3 * sd) * total / n <= 0.8 * cap:
        break
a = 0.995
avail = sum(math.comb(3, j) * a**j * (1 - a)**(3 - j) for j in (2, 3))
print(f"(a) n = {n} (relative sd {sd:.3f}); (b) availability {avail:.6f}; (c) moved {36.5 / (n + 1):.2f} TB primary, {3 * 36.5 / (n + 1):.2f} TB with replicas")
```

```{.text .run-output}
(a) n = 82 (relative sd 0.062); (b) availability 0.999925; (c) moved 0.44 TB primary, 1.32 TB with replicas
```
::::
:::

The second exercise simulates a leaderless store through a node failure. It combines quorums, hinted handoff, version vectors and anti-entropy.

::: {#exr-replication-and-partitioning-int-2}
#### A failure in a leaderless store

Simulate $5$ nodes, $N = 3$, $R = W = 2$, with sloppy quorums and hinted handoff (@def-quorum-replication) and version vectors per key (@def-happens-before). Node $2$ is down for $200$ of $1000$ operations;
during the outage two clients write the same key through different coordinators. Count stale reads, report the versions a read returns after the outage, and check that after handoff and one anti-entropy pass all
replicas agree.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With strict replica sets $R + W > N$ would forbid stale reads (@thm-quorum-intersection); with substitutes during the outage a read can miss a write, although such reads are rare and the run happens to
have none. The two concurrent writes produce incomparable version
vectors, so a read returns both (@thm-logical-clocks (c)) until a client merges them. Hinted handoff returns the substitutes' copies to node $2$, and anti-entropy copies whatever remains, after which every
replica holds the same maximal versions.

## Python

The simulation; versions are dictionaries of per-coordinator counters.

```{.python .run}
import random, zlib
random.seed(47)
nodes, N, R, W = list(range(5)), 3, 2, 2
store = {n: {} for n in nodes}                         # node -> key -> list of (vv, value)
hints = {n: [] for n in nodes}
leq = lambda u, v: all(u.get(k, 0) <= v.get(k, 0) for k in u.keys() | v.keys())
def pref(key):
    s = zlib.crc32(key.encode()) % 5
    return [(s + i) % 5 for i in range(5)]
def add(n, key, vv, val):
    vs = [x for x in store[n].get(key, []) if not leq(x[0], vv)]
    if not any(leq(vv, x[0]) for x in vs):
        vs.append((vv, val))
    store[n][key] = vs
def put(key, val, coord, ctx, down):
    vv = dict(ctx); vv[coord] = vv.get(coord, 0) + 1
    healthy = [n for n in pref(key) if n not in down][:N]
    for n in healthy:
        add(n, key, vv, val)
        if n not in pref(key)[:N]:
            hints[n].append((next(m for m in pref(key)[:N] if m in down), key, vv, val))
    return vv
def get(key, down):
    healthy = [n for n in pref(key) if n not in down][:R]
    vs = [x for n in healthy for x in store[n].get(key, [])]
    return [x for x in vs if not any(leq(x[0], y[0]) and x[0] != y[0] for y in vs)]
latest, stale = {}, 0
for t in range(1000):
    down = {2} if 300 <= t < 500 else set()
    key = f"k{random.randrange(20)}"
    if random.random() < 0.5:
        latest[key] = put(key, t, random.choice([n for n in nodes if n not in down]), {}, down)
    elif key in latest:
        stale += not any(leq(latest[key], x[0]) for x in get(key, down))
    if t == 400:                                        # two concurrent writes to one key
        put("cart", "book", 0, {}, down); put("cart", "pen", 1, {}, down)
print("stale reads:", stale, "| versions of cart after the outage:", sorted({x[1] for x in get("cart", set())}))
for h in nodes:                                         # hinted handoff
    for target, key, vv, val in hints[h]:
        add(target, key, vv, val)
for key in {k for n in nodes for k in store[n]}:        # one anti-entropy pass over each preference list
    reps = pref(key)[:N]
    for a in reps:
        for b in reps:
            for vv, val in list(store[b].get(key, [])):
                add(a, key, vv, val)
agree = all(sorted(map(str, store[a].get(k, []))) == sorted(map(str, store[b].get(k, [])))
            for k in {k for n in nodes for k in store[n]} for a in pref(k)[:N] for b in pref(k)[:N])
print("replicas agree after handoff and anti-entropy:", agree)
```

```{.text .run-output}
stale reads: 0 | versions of cart after the outage: ['book', 'pen']
replicas agree after handoff and anti-entropy: True
```
::::
:::

The third exercise runs a leader failover end to end. It combines detection, failover and identifiers.

::: {#exr-replication-and-partitioning-int-3}
#### A failover with identifiers

A metadata leader issues Snowflake identifiers (@def-unique-id) and replicates semi-synchronously to two followers with $k = 1$ (@def-leader-follower). Heartbeats every $0.25\,\mathrm{s}$ with $k = 3$
(@prp-heartbeat-detector) detect its crash. (a) Bound the detection time with $D = 0.05\,\mathrm{s}$. (b) Which follower must be promoted (@prp-failover-loss), and what must the new leader do so that it never issues
an identifier the old leader issued? (c) Simulate the log, the crash and the promotion, and check that no acknowledged write is lost and no identifier repeats.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

(a) $\theta = 3 \times 0.25 + 0.05 = 0.8\,\mathrm{s}$, so detection within $0.85\,\mathrm{s}$. (b) The follower with the longer log, compared across both since $|F| > f - k = 1$. The new leader runs on a different
machine identifier, so by @prp-id-collision (c) its identifiers differ from the old leader's whatever the clocks say; reusing the old machine identifier would need its last timestamp from the log. (c) The run
checks both properties.

## Python

The log, two followers, a crash after a random acknowledged prefix, and identifiers from two machine numbers.

```{.python .run}
import random
random.seed(48)
EPOCH = 0
def snowflake(machine):
    last, seq = -1, 0
    def nxt(ms):
        nonlocal last, seq
        ms = max(ms, last); seq = seq + 1 if ms == last else 0; last = ms
        return (ms << 22) | (machine << 12) | seq
    return nxt
gen = snowflake(1); log, f = [], [0, 0]; acked = 0; ids = []
for i in range(1, 501):
    pid = gen(i // 4); log.append(pid); ids.append(pid)
    j = random.randrange(2); f[j] = i                          # k = 1: one follower stores it before the ack
    if random.random() < 0.5: f[1 - j] = max(f[1 - j], random.randint(f[1 - j], i))
    acked = i
new = max(range(2), key=lambda j: f[j])
print("acknowledged", acked, "| promoted follower has", f[new], "| lost acknowledged writes:", acked - f[new])
gen2 = snowflake(2)
ids += [gen2(i // 4) for i in range(500, 700)]
print("identifiers issued", len(ids), "| repeats", len(ids) - len(set(ids)))
```

```{.text .run-output}
acknowledged 500 | promoted follower has 500 | lost acknowledged writes: 0
identifiers issued 700 | repeats 0
```
